key_contribution: LaTee, an amortized EM framework that uses GFlowNets to perform diverse Bayesian inference over symbolic logic trees generated by LLMs, achieving ~25% relative error reduction over SOTA attention-based temporal point process models on healthcare event prediction while providing interpretable rule-based explanations.
limitations: Resource constraints limited experiments to models up to 6.7B parameters and event sequences of at most 40 events, with very small dataset sizes (142–477 sequences) and high variance in results (e.g., 8.66% std on MIMIC-3). Scalability to larger predicate spaces, longer sequences, and larger LLMs remains unverified, and the non-semantic StackOverflow result does not clearly outperform the strongest baseline.
surprise_factor: The ~25% relative error reduction over AttNHP on MIMIC-3 is notable, but the evidence is thin: datasets contain only 142–477 sequences, results are averaged over three seeds with large variance (e.g., 8.66% std on MIMIC-3), and the StackOverflow result actually underperforms AttNHP. The conceptual insight that GFlowNet's diversity-seeking objective produces broader rule coverage than SFT/PPO is reasonable given the design but not deeply surprising. No particularly surprising findings overall — a promising method combination validated on small-scale experiments.

title: Generative Enzyme Design Guided by Functionally Important Sites and Small-Molecule Substrates
task_novelty_note: Enzyme design exists for specific families (PROTSEED, RFDiffusion); this paper extends it to a unified cross-family model with substrate conditioning.

compares_to.title: Protein sequence and structure co-design with equivariant translation
compares_to.evidence: Listed as PROTSEED baseline in Tables 2, 3, and 4 with ESP scores, binding affinities, and pLDDT values alongside EnzyGen

compares_to.title: De novo design of protein structure and function with rfdiffusion
compares_to.evidence: Listed as RFDiffusion+IF baseline in Tables 2, 3, and 4; RFDiffusion generates the structure which is then inverse-folded by ProteinMPNN

compares_to.title: Robust deep learning-based protein sequence design using proteinmpnn
compares_to.evidence: ProteinMPNN (IF) is the inverse folding component of the RFDiffusion+IF baseline pipeline in Tables 2, 3, and 4

compares_to.title: Language models of protein sequences at the scale of evolution enable accurate structure prediction
compares_to.evidence: ESM2 is the sequence encoder in the ESM2+EGNN baseline listed in Tables 2, 3, and 4

compares_to.title: E(n) equivariant graph neural networks
compares_to.evidence: EGNN is the backbone structure predictor in the ESM2+EGNN baseline listed in Tables 2, 3, and 4

key_contribution: EnzyGen, a unified generative model that jointly designs enzyme amino acid sequences and 3D backbone structures across 3,157 enzyme families by interleaving global Transformer attention with SE(3)-equivariant neighborhood message passing (NAEL), conditioned on automatically mined functionally important sites and small-molecule substrates, achieving the best average substrate binding affinity (−9.44 kcal/mol), ESP score (0.65), and AlphaFold2 pLDDT (87.45) across 323 testing families.
limitations: The dataset covers only 3,157 of 8,422 fourth-level EC categories (restricted to those with experimentally confirmed PDB structures), and the substrate constraint is limited to a binary enzyme-substrate binding prediction rather than explicit 3D complex pose design, which the authors note is relatively weak for capturing catalytic function.
surprise_factor: The zero-shot generalization to two unseen substrates and two unseen fourth-level categories (average ESP 0.83–0.89, >85% above the 0.6 binding threshold) is mildly surprising, suggesting functionally important sites carry substantial transferable information, though the evidence is limited to four test cases. The overall performance gains over strong baselines (10.79% in binding affinity, consistent across all 30 third-level categories) are solid but within the range expected for a well-motivated architectural addition (substrate constraint + interleaved attention/equivariant layers).

title: Position: A Roadmap to Pluralistic Alignment
task_novelty_note: Extends standard AI alignment (single averaged human preference) to a multi-dimensional pluralistic formulation with three formalized sub-tasks.

compares_to.title: Llama 2: Open foundation and fine-tuned chat models
compares_to.evidence: LLaMA and LLaMA2 (pre) and LLaMA2-Chat (post) appear in Table 1 with Jensen-Shannon distance values compared to human distributions

compares_to.title: Stanford alpaca: An instruction-following llama model
compares_to.evidence: Alpaca (post-aligned LLaMA) appears in Table 1 with JSD values for GlobalQA and MPI, compared against pre-aligned LLaMA

compares_to.title: How far can camels go? exploring the state of instruction tuning on open resources
compares_to.evidence: Tulu (post-aligned LLaMA) appears in Table 1 with JSD values for GlobalQA and MPI, compared against pre-aligned LLaMA

compares_to.title: Gemma: Open models based on gemini research and technology
compares_to.evidence: Gemma 7B (pre) and Gemma 7B IT (post) appear in Table 1 with JSD values compared to human distributions

compares_to.title: OpenAI davinci-002 model
compares_to.evidence: GPT-3 davinci-002 (pre) and GPT-3.5-turbo (post) appear in Table 1 with JSD values for GlobalQA and MPI

key_contribution: Formalizes three definitions of pluralistic AI models (Overton, steerable, and distributional) and three corresponding benchmark types (multi-objective, trade-off steerable, and jury-pluralistic), and provides empirical evidence across LLaMA, LLaMA2, Gemma, and GPT-3 that standard alignment procedures (RLHF, instruction fine-tuning) consistently reduce distributional pluralism by increasing Jensen-Shannon distance to human population distributions and decreasing output entropy.
limitations: The empirical evaluation is limited to two multiple-choice datasets (GlobalOpinionQA and MPI) with 5-prompt averaging, and the authors explicitly note that 'a more comprehensive investigation of this hypothesis requires large-scale experimentation across a broader range of domains.' Several of the formal definitions (e.g., operationalizing the Overton window, selecting a target population) are acknowledged as 'hard to operationalize,' and the GPT-3 comparison is flagged as unreliable due to uncertainty about the exact alignment procedure applied to GPT-3.5-turbo.
surprise_factor: The consistency of the distributional-entropy reduction across four model families is notable, but it largely confirms and extends prior findings from Santurkar et al. and Durmus et al.; the evidence base (two multiple-choice datasets, 5-prompt averaging, questionable GPT-3 baseline) limits the strength of the claim. The conceptual contribution (three distinct pluralism types) is more a useful reframing than a surprising result.

title: Position: Opportunities Exist for Machine Learning in Magnetic Fusion Energy
task_novelty_note: All six tasks (disruption prediction, plasma control, equilibrium reconstruction, etc.) are well-established in the fusion literature; the paper surveys them rather than introducing new problem formulations.
key_contribution: First comprehensive position paper targeting the ML community with a structured roadmap of six high-impact research challenges in tokamak fusion (disruption prediction, simulation/dynamics modeling, partial observability, control, optimal experiment design, and materials discovery), reviewing prior ML work for each and identifying concrete technical barriers and future opportunities as fusion data infrastructure matures.
limitations: As a position paper, it proposes and evaluates no new methods or models, and its future-opportunity section (foundation models, federated learning, multi-modal fusion) is explicitly speculative pending data infrastructure upgrades. The paper acknowledges that institutional data-access barriers and the fragmented 'archipelago' nature of fusion datasets remain unresolved, limiting immediate practical applicability of the identified opportunities.
surprise_factor: No particularly surprising findings, as this is a position/survey paper with no experimental results. The main conceptual point—that fusion data infrastructure is a 'archipelago' of narrow, institutionally siloed datasets rather than a unified corpus, and that this is the primary bottleneck for ML impact—is a well-known frustration in the fusion community but is articulated here with unusual clarity for an ML audience.

title: Offline Actor-Critic Reinforcement Learning Scales to Large Models
task_novelty_note: Extends offline actor-critic RL from small single-task models to ~1B parameter multi-task, multi-modal transformers with scaling law analysis.

builds_on.title: Perceiver: General perception with iterative attention
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we adopt the methodology from the perceiver model (Jaegle et al., 2021)' to shift self-attention from input sequence to latent vectors, forming the core encoder backbone.

builds_on.title: Perceiver IO: A general architecture for structured inputs & outputs
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'querying information from zM is again implemented via cross-attention following the decoding architecture of Perceiver-IO (Jaegle et al., 2022)' for both policy and Q-value decoding.

builds_on.title: Multi-Objective Policy Optimization (MPO)
builds_on.evidence: Paper states the proposed algorithm 'can be seen as a simplified variant of MPO/DIME (Abdolmaleki et al., 2018; 2022)' for the KL-regularized policy optimization objective.

builds_on.title: On multiobjective policy optimization as a tool for reinforcement learning: Case studies in offline rl and finetuning (DIME)
builds_on.evidence: Paper states the algorithm is 'a simplified variant of MPO/DIME (Abdolmaleki et al., 2018; 2022)' and 'Like prior work (Abdolmaleki et al., 2022; Fujimoto & Gu, 2021), we combine a BC regularization term with an off-policy RL method.'

builds_on.title: A distributional perspective on reinforcement learning
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we employ tools from the distributional reinforcement learning literature (Bellemare et al., 2017) which transform the problem of learning Qθ into minimizing the negative log likelihood of a discretized Q-function distribution' and uses the distributional TD operator.

builds_on.title: A minimalist approach to offline reinforcement learning
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Like prior work (Abdolmaleki et al., 2022; Fujimoto & Gu, 2021), we combine a BC regularization term with an off-policy RL method' and cites it as prior example for using BC loss as regularization in offline RL.

compares_to.title: A generalist agent (Gato)
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'BC(Gato†)' baseline with 63.6% expert reward on Gato:Control, directly compared against PAC's 87.7%.

compares_to.title: RoboCat: A self-improving foundation agent for robotic manipulation
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'BC(RC★)' baseline with 61.0%, 64.5%, 71.3% success rates on RC:Tower, RC:Pyramid, RC:Insertion respectively, directly compared against PAC.

compares_to.title: Q-transformer: Scalable offline reinforcement learning via autoregressive q-functions
compares_to.evidence: Paper states 'We provide an additional comparison to a Q-transformer (Chebotar et al., 2023) baseline' with numerical results in Appendix Table 14 comparing against PAC on Control Suite tasks.

key_contribution: Demonstrates that offline actor-critic reinforcement learning follows Chinchilla-style scaling laws and outperforms behavioral cloning baselines when scaled to ~1B-parameter Perceiver-based transformers, enabling stable multi-task control from sub-optimal data via a simple BC-to-RL interpolation parameter.
limitations: Offline RL requires reward annotations, which can be costly in robotics, and the wide variety of domains considered showed no strong indications of cross-task transfer, suggesting that dataset composition and overlap will be critical for future scaling.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is conceptual: offline RL not only scales but scales *better* with compute than BC (parameter exponent 0.92 vs 0.83), which challenges the assumption that RL's additional optimization complexity would hinder scaling. This is well-supported by a systematic 5-scale analysis following Chinchilla methodology. The CHEF result (55% success from 28%-quality data vs 17% for BC) is a strong but expected demonstration of RL's advantage on sub-optimal data.

title: CHEMREASONER: Heuristic Search over a Large Language Model's Knowledge Space using Quantum-Chemical Feedback
task_novelty_note: Catalyst discovery/screening is a well-established task in computational chemistry; the paper contributes a new LLM-guided search method with quantum-chemical feedback for it.

builds_on.title: Monte Carlo Thought Search: Large Language Model Querying for Complex Scientific Reasoning in Catalyst Design
builds_on.evidence: Paper explicitly states 'Our work follows the catalysis-focused approach of Sprueill et al. (2023)' and 'our method builds upon Sprueill et al. (2023), Unlike their approach...we integrate true computational chemistry-based rewards to guide the model.'

builds_on.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Heuristic searches have been applied for general problem solving and reasoning tasks for LLMs (Yao et al., 2023)' and adapts the tree search structure with beam pruning, replacing LLM-computed rewards with quantum-chemistry-based rewards.

compares_to.title: Chain of Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'Chain-of-Thought' baseline with numerical reward values across all three query categories (OpenCatalyst, BioFuels, CO2-Conversion) for both GPT-4 and GPT-3.5.

key_contribution: An AI-guided catalyst discovery framework (CHEMREASONER) that unifies LLM-driven heuristic tree search with quantum-chemical GNN feedback (adsorption energies and reaction pathway barriers) as domain-grounded rewards, demonstrating that a fully automated planner can match or exceed expert-enumerated chemical descriptor search strategies in 2 of 3 query categories.
limitations: The text-to-3D-structure conversion is restricted to FCC/BCC/HCP lattice templates with random element substitution, which may not accurately represent realistic multimetallic catalyst structures, and GNN-predicted adsorption energies diverge substantially from DFT ground truth (e.g., 0.384 eV GNN vs. -0.066 eV DFT for CO2 on CuZn), undermining confidence in absolute reward values. The system also depends on proprietary LLMs (GPT-3.5/GPT-4) whose instruction-following robustness is critical for the pipeline's reliability.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is that the fully automated planner (zero expert input) outperforms expert-enumerated chemical descriptors in 2 of 3 query categories, suggesting that LLM contextual reasoning can substitute for domain-expert search design. However, the evidence is limited to 145 queries and two proprietary LLMs, and the GNN-vs-DFT divergence (e.g., 0.384 eV GNN vs. -0.066 eV DFT for CO2 on CuZn) undermines confidence in the absolute reward values, tempering the practical significance of the ranking improvements.

title: Contextual Feature Selection with Conditional Stochastic Gates
task_novelty_note: Extends population-level feature selection to context-conditioned selection via hypernetwork-parameterized stochastic gates, generalizing prior contextual methods (CEN, Contextual LASSO) to non-linear predictors and l0-like sparsity.

builds_on.title: Feature selection using stochastic gates
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We utilize a Gaussian-based relaxation for Bernoulli variables, termed Stochastic Gates (STG) (Yamada et al., 2020)' and directly extends STG by conditioning the gate parameters on context variables via a hypernetwork

compares_to.title: Regression shrinkage and selection via the lasso
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'LASSO' baseline with accuracy/R2 numbers across all five datasets

compares_to.title: Feature selection using stochastic gates
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'STG' baseline with accuracy/R2 numbers across all five datasets

compares_to.title: Contextual explanation networks
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'CEN' baseline with accuracy/R2 numbers across all five datasets

compares_to.title: The contextual lasso: Sparse linear models via deep neural networks
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'Contextual LASSO' baseline with accuracy/R2 numbers across all five datasets

compares_to.title: Learning to maximize mutual information for dynamic feature selection
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'AFS' baseline with accuracy/R2 numbers across all five datasets

compares_to.title: Invase: Instancewise variable selection using neural networks
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'INVASE' baseline with accuracy/R2 numbers across all five datasets

key_contribution: A novel end-to-end framework (c-STG) that uses a hypernetwork to condition stochastic feature selection gates on contextual variables, enabling a single model to adaptively select different informative features per context while achieving sparser and more accurate predictions than population-level and existing contextual feature selection methods.
limitations: The paper explicitly acknowledges that parameter tuning (particularly the regularization coefficient λ) lacks the well-established theoretical guidance available for LASSO, making hyperparameter selection a practical bottleneck. Additionally, the method relies on Monte Carlo sampling during training which introduces variance, and the empirical evaluation is limited to relatively small-scale datasets (e.g., ~300-sample UCI heart disease, MNIST subset of two digits).
surprise_factor: The most notable result is the neuroscience application where a single weighted c-STG model replicates findings previously requiring 7,866 separate SVM classifiers, but this is more a practical efficiency win than a conceptual surprise. Performance improvements over baselines are consistent but incremental (e.g., 89.23% vs 87.88% on heart disease), and the theoretical results (STG parameters equal expectations of c-STG parameters) are clean but expected given the nested feasible spaces. No particularly surprising findings overall.

title: The Fundamental Limits of Least-Privilege Learning
task_novelty_note: Extends single-attribute obfuscation to the full LPP (all attributes, conditional on Y with fundamental leakage), which prior work only stated informally.

builds_on.title: The conditional entropy bottleneck
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Our formalisation of the LPP is closely related to the Minimum Necessary Information (MNI) principle introduced by Fischer (2020)' and 'can be seen as a variant of the conditional entropy bottleneck (CEB) problem (Fischer, 2020)'

builds_on.title: An operational approach to information leakage
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Notably, the quantity constrained by the LPP is known as maximal leakage (Issa et al., 2019)' and uses its closed-form properties as the core leakage measure in the formalization

compares_to.title: Gradient Reversal Against Discrimination
compares_to.evidence: GRAD censoring appears in Fig. 4 (bottom) with numerical inference gain results in the same heatmaps and bar charts as standard ERM, showing the LPP trade-off holds for this censoring technique

compares_to.title: Trade-offs and guarantees of adversarial representation learning for information obfuscation
compares_to.evidence: MAX-ENT adversarial representation learning appears in Fig. 6 with numerical inference gain results on the Adult dataset, evaluated alongside the same utility metric to confirm the LPP trade-off

key_contribution: First formalization of the least-privilege principle for machine learning as a variant of the conditional entropy bottleneck, proving a fundamental impossibility: under a strictly positive posterior, no feature representation can simultaneously achieve utility I_α(Y;Z) > γ and satisfy the LPP with parameter γ, regardless of the learning technique or architecture.
limitations: The impossibility result relies on Assumption A (strictly positive posterior), and the trade-off could be less stringent for distributions where this assumption does not hold. The leakage measure (maximal leakage over all possible attributes) is the strongest possible; restricting the adversary's target class (e.g., to 'efficiently identifiable' attributes) might yield a more favorable trade-off but would deviate from the LPP's 'nothing else' promise.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that a widely-endorsed principle (LPL) is provably unachievable under mild, realistic assumptions — the 'whack-a-mole' effect where censoring one attribute increases leakage of another is a strong negative result that challenges the field's working assumption that representation learning can separate task-relevant from task-irrelevant information. The evidence is strong: a clean theoretical proof backed by empirical validation across multiple datasets, architectures, learning techniques, and MLaaS settings.

title: Diffusion Models Encode the Intrinsic Dimension of Data Manifolds
task_novelty_note: Intrinsic dimension estimation is a well-studied task dating to Fukunaga & Olsen (1971); the paper contributes a new method rather than a new problem formulation.

builds_on.title: Score-based generative modeling through stochastic differential equations
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'In (Song et al., 2020) score-based and diffusion-based generative models were unified into a single continuous-time score-based framework' and the entire method relies on the score function approximation from this SDE framework to estimate the normal bundle

compares_to.title: Intrinsic dimensionality estimation using normalizing flows
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as ID-NF baseline with numerical dimension estimates across all datasets

compares_to.title: Maximum likelihood estimation of intrinsic dimension
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as MLE(m=5) and MLE(m=20) baselines with numerical dimension estimates

compares_to.title: Translated poisson mixture model for stratification learning
compares_to.evidence: Cited alongside Levina and Bickel as the MLE estimator used in Table 2 comparisons

compares_to.title: Intrinsic dimension estimation of data by principal component analysis
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as Local PCA baseline with numerical dimension estimates across all datasets

compares_to.title: Automatic choice of dimensionality for pca
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as PPCA baseline with numerical dimension estimates across all datasets

compares_to.title: Probabilistic principal component analysis
compares_to.evidence: Cited alongside Minka as the PPCA framework used in Table 2 comparisons

key_contribution: Proves that the score function of a diffusion model at vanishing noise aligns with the normal bundle of the data manifold, and leverages this geometric insight to propose the first diffusion-based intrinsic dimension estimator that outperforms PCA, MLE, and normalizing-flow methods on high-dimensional non-linear manifolds.
limitations: The method requires a pre-trained diffusion model and is inherently local, necessitating multiple pointwise evaluations and taking the maximum to account for geometric and approximation errors. The theoretical guarantee assumes the data distribution is strictly supported on a smooth compact manifold, and the method can underestimate dimension for extremely non-uniform distributions or when data is only concentrated around (rather than contained in) the manifold.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is moderate: the rigorous proof that the score function at vanishing noise aligns with the normal bundle is elegant but somewhat anticipated by the score's role as a gradient of log-density. More notably, the empirical challenge to Pope et al.'s MNIST ID estimate (~14 via MLE vs. ~152 via diffusion) is a significant discrepancy that, if confirmed, would revise a commonly cited number in the field. However, the MNIST result lacks ground truth and relies on auto-encoder reconstruction curves as validation, which weakens the claim somewhat.

title: Grokking Group Multiplication with Cosets
task_novelty_note: Reverse engineering group multiplication networks was already established by Chughtai et al.; this paper re-examines the same task with a different proposed circuit.

builds_on.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Our work builds directly on A Toy Model of Universality by Chughtai et al. [4]. We recreated precisely their experimental setup for the groups S5 and S6.'

compares_to.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering How Networks Learn Group Operations
compares_to.evidence: Paper explicitly compares its coset circuit interpretation against the GCR algorithm proposed in [4], providing evidence in Section 7 that the GCR algorithm does not explain observed behaviors (coset concentration, ReLU-to-absolute-value improvement) while the coset circuit does.

key_contribution: Complete reverse engineering of one-hidden-layer networks that have grokked group multiplication in S5 and S6, revealing that the model implements 'coset circuits' exploiting the true subgroup/coset structure of the symmetric group rather than the previously proposed matrix-irrep multiplication algorithm, validated through targeted causal interventions.
limitations: The analysis is restricted to a single hidden layer, fully-connected architecture on the small groups S5 and S6, which the authors explicitly note is a 'toy problem' and that 'interpreting real models will be even difficult.' The methodology's generalizability to deeper architectures, larger groups, or real-world models remains untested.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that the model does not implement the elegant GCR algorithm (matrix multiplication of irreps) previously identified for this exact setup, but instead uses a more combinatorial coset-membership mechanism; additionally, the fact that two papers on the same model produced irreconcilable interpretations underscores how fragile correlational interpretability evidence can be, even in a fully controlled setting.

title: Harmonic Self-Conditioned Flow Matching for joint Multi-Ligand Docking and Binding Site Design
task_novelty_note: Pocket design exists (PocketOptimizer, DEFACT) but requires the bound complex; this extends it to joint docking+design without 3D structure and to multi-ligands.

builds_on.title: Flow Matching for Generative Modeling
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we develop HARMONICFLOW, an improved generative process over 3D protein-ligand binding structures based on our self-conditioned flow matching objective' and uses the conditional flow matching loss from this work as the core training framework

builds_on.title: Analog Bits: Generating Discrete Data Using Diffusion Models with Self-Conditioning
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we achieve the same by adapting the discrete diffusion model self-conditioning approach of Chen et al. (2023)' for the structure self-conditioning mechanism

builds_on.title: EigenFold: Generative Protein Structure Prediction with Diffusion Models
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We choose a harmonic prior as in EigenFold (Jing et al., 2023) that samples atoms to be close to each other if they are connected by a bond'

builds_on.title: PiFold: Toward Effective and Efficient Protein Inverse Folding
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we construct on PiFold's (Gao et al., 2023a) distance-based invariant edge features and node features that encode the geometry of the backbone' for the invariant network component

compares_to.title: DiffDock: Diffusion Steps, Twists, and Turns for Molecular Docking
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'PRODUCT SPACE DIFFUSION' baseline with RMSD and %<2 metrics on PDBBind docking, and in Tables 6 and 7 for additional docking comparisons

compares_to.title: EigenFold: Generative Protein Structure Prediction with Diffusion Models
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as 'EIGENFOLD DIFFUSION' baseline for multi-ligand docking on Binding MOAD with %<2, %<5, and median RMSD metrics

compares_to.title: Robust Deep Learning-Based Protein Sequence Design Using ProteinMPNN
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 3 as 'PROTEINMPNN (no ligand)' baseline for binding site recovery with BLOSUM score and recovery metrics

compares_to.title: PiFold: Toward Effective and Efficient Protein Inverse Folding
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 3 as 'PIFOLD (no ligand)' and 'PIFOLD (2D ligand)' baselines for binding site recovery with BLOSUM score and recovery metrics

compares_to.title: DiffDock-Pocket: Diffusion for Pocket-Level Docking with Sidechain Flexibility
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 3 as 'DIFFDOCK-POCKET POS' baseline for binding site recovery where ligand positions are given by the DiffDock-Pocket docking tool

key_contribution: Introduces HARMONICFLOW, a self-conditioned flow matching process with a harmonic prior that generates 3D ligand binding structures by directly updating Cartesian coordinates, and FLOWSITE, which extends this to jointly generate discrete residue types and continuous ligand positions—providing the first deep learning solution for designing protein binding pockets for small molecules (including multi-ligands) without prior knowledge of the ligand's 3D structure.
limitations: All evaluation is computational (sequence recovery, BLOSUM score, RMSD) with no wet-lab validation of actual binding affinity, and the main results are pocket-level rather than blind docking (which is only preliminary in the appendix). The gap to the oracle method (47.0% vs 51.4% recovery on Binding MOAD) indicates the jointly generated structures and residue types are not yet optimal, and the Binding MOAD dataset construction contained a noted error in ligand selection.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that a remarkably simple approach—flow matching directly on Cartesian coordinates with a harmonic prior—outperforms the more structured product-space diffusion of DiffDock (which explicitly models torsions, rotation, and translation) in average sample quality, without any separate structural losses or torsion updates. The ablation showing that equivariant layers are substantially worse than invariant layers for discrete residue type prediction (35.3% vs 47.0% recovery) is also a useful counterintuitive finding, as equivariant architectures are typically preferred for 3D structure tasks.

title: Dirichlet Flow Matching with Applications to DNA Sequence Design
task_novelty_note: DNA sequence generation and conditional design are well-established tasks tackled by autoregressive LMs, D3PM, DDSM, and Bit Diffusion; the contribution is a new method, not a new problem.

builds_on.title: Flow matching for generative modeling
builds_on.evidence: The entire method is a flow matching framework adapted to the simplex: 'Flow matching (FM) is a generative modeling framework that provides a simulation-free means of training continuous normalizing flows' and the paper extends it to discrete categorical data via Dirichlet probability paths.

builds_on.title: Classifier-free diffusion guidance
builds_on.evidence: The paper adapts classifier-free guidance to Dirichlet FM: 'Initially proposed in the context of diffusion models... We implement guidance for Dirichlet FM by deriving a similar relationship between the score and flow field.'

builds_on.title: Flow matching in latent space
builds_on.evidence: The paper derives an analogous score-flow relationship for Dirichlet paths: 'Dao et al. (2023); Zheng et al. (2023) derived a relationship between the score and marginal flow for certain Gaussian probability paths... We implement guidance for Dirichlet FM by deriving a similar relationship.'

builds_on.title: Progressive distillation for fast sampling of diffusion models
builds_on.evidence: The paper applies standard distillation to Dirichlet FM: 'The aim of distillation (Salimans & Ho, 2022; Song et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2023) is to reduce the inference time... we can employ standard distillation approaches and distill the teacher model into a student model.'

compares_to.title: Analog bits: Generating discrete data using diffusion models with self-conditioning
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'BIT DIFFUSION (BIT-ENCODING)' and 'BIT DIFFUSION (ONE-HOT ENCODING)' with MSE values .0414 and .0395 compared against Dirichlet FM's .0269.

compares_to.title: Structured denoising diffusion models in discrete state-spaces
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'D3PM-Uniform' with MSE .0375 compared against Dirichlet FM's .0269.

compares_to.title: Dirichlet diffusion score model for biological sequence generation
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as 'DDSM' with MSE .0334 compared against Dirichlet FM's .0269; also the primary related simplex-based method the paper positions itself against.

key_contribution: Introduces Dirichlet flow matching, a flow matching framework for discrete categorical sequences that uses Dirichlet distributions as conditional probability paths on the simplex (avoiding the shrinking-support pathology of linear FM), derives a linear score-flow relationship enabling classifier(-free) guidance, and demonstrates one-step generation via distillation, achieving state-of-the-art results on DNA promoter and enhancer sequence design.
limitations: Evaluation is confined to three DNA datasets (promoter, fly brain enhancer, melanoma enhancer) using a shared architecture from DDSM, and the method is only demonstrated on 4-category (DNA) data, leaving open whether the Dirichlet path and guidance framework transfer to other discrete domains (text, protein sequences, graphs) or to substantially higher-dimensional simplices. The paper does not include an explicit limitations section.
surprise_factor: The clean theoretical result that linear FM on the simplex necessarily loses support over vertices at predictable times (t > 1/k) is a satisfying negative result that explains why the most natural approach fails, and the Dirichlet path is a minimal, well-motivated fix. The empirical FBD gap with classifier-free guidance (1.9 vs. 36.0) is large, but the scope is limited to three DNA datasets with a shared architecture, so the magnitude should be read with some caution.

title: Partial Optimality in the Linear Ordering Problem
task_novelty_note: The linear ordering problem is a well-established NP-hard task; the contribution is new partial-optimality conditions and algorithms for it.

builds_on.title: Exact and Partial Energy Minimization in Computer Vision
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we characterize and search for improving maps, a technique introduced by Shekhovtsov (2013)' — the entire partial optimality framework is derived from this improving maps technique.

builds_on.title: Maximum persistency in energy minimization
builds_on.evidence: Cited as part of the improving maps/persistency technique lineage: 'a technique introduced by Shekhovtsov (2013); see also Shekhovtsov (2014)'

builds_on.title: Maximum persistency via iterative relaxed inference with graphical models
builds_on.evidence: Cited as part of the improving maps/persistency technique lineage: 'see also Shekhovtsov et al. (2015)' — the iterative application of partial optimality conditions follows this work.

key_contribution: Introduces four families of improving maps (transposition, grouping, conditional grouping, shifting) with efficiently testable sufficient conditions that certify partial optimality for the NP-hard linear ordering problem, fixing 10–90% of variables on LOLIB benchmark instances and reducing branch-and-cut solving time by up to a factor of 33.
limitations: The most effective condition (conditional grouping, Proposition 4.11) requires solving O(|A|²) max-flow problems and is roughly three orders of magnitude slower than the simpler grouping condition, while the shifting conditions contribute only marginally to the fraction of fixed variables. The authors note that exploiting sparsity of non-zero cost coefficients and extending the framework to the partial ordering problem remain open directions.
surprise_factor: No particularly surprising findings—the speed-ups (1/13 to 1/33) and variable-fixing rates (10–90% on IO) are consistent with what one would expect from well-designed persistency conditions on structured combinatorial problems. The practical trade-off that the most effective condition (conditional grouping, Prop. 4.11) is three orders of magnitude slower than the simplest (grouping, Prop. 4.8) is a useful but unsurprising observation.

title: Towards Compositionality in Concept Learning
task_novelty_note: Extends unsupervised concept extraction by adding compositionality as an explicit design and evaluation criterion, which prior methods neither enforced nor measured.

compares_to.title: Representation engineering: A top-down approach to ai transparency
compares_to.evidence: Listed as PCA baseline in Table 2a, Table 2, Table 3, and Figure 6 with MAP, compositionality score, cosine similarity, and downstream accuracy numbers

compares_to.title: Towards automatic concept-based explanations
compares_to.evidence: Listed as ACE (KMeans) baseline in Table 2a, Table 2, Table 3, and Figure 6 with MAP, compositionality score, cosine similarity, and downstream accuracy numbers

compares_to.title: Towards monosemanticity: Decomposing language models with dictionary learning
compares_to.evidence: Listed as DictLearn baseline in Table 2a, Table 2, Table 3, and Figure 6 with MAP, compositionality score, cosine similarity, and downstream accuracy numbers

compares_to.title: Craft: Concept recursive activation factorization for explainability
compares_to.evidence: Listed as SemiNMF baseline in Table 2a, Table 2, Table 3, and Figure 6 with MAP, compositionality score, cosine similarity, and downstream accuracy numbers

compares_to.title: Attention-based interpretability with concept transformers
compares_to.evidence: Listed as CT (Concept Transformer) baseline in Table 2a, Table 2, Table 3, and Figure 6 with MAP, compositionality score, cosine similarity, and downstream accuracy numbers

key_contribution: Identifies that existing unsupervised concept extraction methods produce non-compositional concepts, proves that orthogonality across attributes and non-orthogonality within attributes are necessary for compositionality, and proposes Compositional Concept Extraction (CCE) which enforces these properties by jointly learning subspaces via orthogonal rejection, achieving ground-truth-level compositionality scores and improved downstream classification accuracy across vision and language datasets.
limitations: The paper assumes a flat concept structure and only studies compositional concepts, leaving non-compositional concepts (e.g., 'hot dog') and hierarchical structures (e.g., '(small blue) car' vs 'small (blue car)') to future work. Additionally, discovered concept vectors require manual naming through inspection of top-scoring samples, which does not scale to large numbers of concepts.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is the disconnect between individual concept quality and compositional quality: methods like NMF and PCA achieve high ROC-AUC on individual concepts yet their compositions are essentially random, a gap made vivid by the toy example in Figure 3. However, the theoretical explanation (high-dimensional orthogonality across attributes) is fairly predictable from concentration-of-measure arguments, and CCE's practical gains over the best baselines on non-synthetic datasets are modest, so the overall surprise is moderate.

title: Learning to Intervene on Concept Bottlenecks
task_novelty_note: Extends the existing CBM intervention task (Koh et al., 2020) from single-sample corrections to cross-sample generalization and bottleneck-specific error detection.

builds_on.title: Concept Bottleneck Models
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'CB2Ms are based on adding a two-fold memory of interventions to the CBM architecture' and 'The bottleneck and predictor networks of the CBM remain unchanged but are extended by a two-fold memory module'

compares_to.title: Concept Bottleneck Models
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Tables 1 and 4 as the base CBM baseline with concept and class accuracy numbers alongside CB2M

compares_to.title: A baseline for detecting misclassified and out-of-distribution examples in neural networks
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Tables 2 and 3 as the 'Softmax' baseline for mistake detection with AUROC and AUPR values alongside CB2M

key_contribution: Introduces Concept Bottleneck Memory Models (CB2Ms), which extend CBMs with a two-fold memory (mistake memory and intervention memory) to generalize human interventions to unseen examples and proactively detect bottleneck errors, reducing the need for repeated human feedback while maintaining interpretability.
limitations: The method assumes human-provided interventions are correct, which may not hold with malicious or unreliable users. Additionally, the nearest-neighbor memory approach may face scalability challenges in large-scale deployments, and high variance in concept encodings can increase the number of required interventions.
surprise_factor: The most notable result is the near-complete recovery on confounded Parity C-MNIST, where concept accuracy jumps from ~80% (near random) to ~100% on identified instances via a simple nearest-neighbor memory — but this follows logically from the mechanism correcting a systematic bottleneck failure. The finding that 25% of validation interventions already yield substantial gains is practically useful but not deeply surprising given the systematic-error framing.

title: QORA: Zero-Shot Transfer via Interpretable Object-Relational Model Learning
task_novelty_note: Object-oriented transition modeling without domain knowledge is already addressed by NPE and MHDPA; QORA provides a new method for this established task.

compares_to.title: A compositional object-based approach to learning physical dynamics
compares_to.evidence: Figure 1a shows NPE (Neural Physics Engine) error curves alongside QORA on the walls domain; Figure 6 compares QORA runtime to NPE runtime directly

compares_to.title: Attention is all you need
compares_to.evidence: Figure 1a shows MHDPA (Multi-Head Dot Product Attention) error curves alongside QORA on the walls domain as a neural-network baseline

key_contribution: QORA, a domain-agnostic algorithm that learns interpretable first-order-logic transition rules from object-oriented observations via iterative predicate combination guided by Occam's Razor and a novel bit-string encoding of quantified formulas, achieving ~10,000× better sample efficiency than neural baselines with zero-shot transfer to larger environments.
limitations: The evaluation is limited to relatively simple grid-world domains with small integer-valued attributes and a small number of object classes; the paper acknowledges that developing a full theoretical model of QORA's sample and runtime complexity is an open problem, and the method's applicability to continuous attribute spaces, high-dimensional environments, or real-world perception tasks remains untested.
surprise_factor: The ~10,000× sample-efficiency gap over neural baselines is large, but the comparison is on very simple grid-worlds with small, under-tuned networks (6,944 and 2,784 parameters), so the gap likely narrows substantially on harder domains. The more interesting conceptual point—that a symbolic/statistical method can achieve perfect zero-shot transfer to 128×128 worlds with ~5,000 objects while producing human-readable rules—is a meaningful challenge to the assumption that neural networks are necessary for structured world modeling, though it is not entirely unexpected given the rule-based nature of the test domains.

title: Private Truly-Everlasting Robust-Prediction
task_novelty_note: Extends PEP (Naor et al. 2023) by adding adversarial robustness and a time-varying δ that removes the T-dependence, making the prediction truly unbounded.

builds_on.title: Private everlasting prediction
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We present two conceptual modifications to the definition of PEP' and 'we observe that the construction of Naor et al. (2023) can be adjusted to satisfy our new definition of PERP', directly extending the PEP framework and its generic construction.

builds_on.title: Optimal differentially private learning of thresholds and quasi-concave optimization
builds_on.evidence: The RectanglesPERP algorithm directly uses the Reorder-Slice-Compute (RSC) paradigm from this paper as a core subroutine (Algorithm 1), without which the adaptive slicing of the dataset would not work.

builds_on.title: Make up your mind: The price of online queries in differential privacy
builds_on.evidence: The BetweenThresholds algorithm (Algorithm 3) from this paper is a core component of the ChallengeBT subroutine, which is central to the RectanglesPERP construction for privately answering threshold queries.

builds_on.title: On the complexity of differentially private data release: efficient algorithms and hardness results
builds_on.evidence: The Stopper algorithm (Algorithm 2) is described as 'a special case of the classical AboveThreshold algorithm of Dwork et al. (2009), also known as the Sparse Vector Technique' and is a core component of ChallengeBT.

key_contribution: Introduces robustness against adversarial poisoning queries and a time-varying privacy parameter δ into the Private Everlasting Prediction framework, yielding computationally efficient constructions for axis-aligned rectangles and decision-stumps with sample complexity linear in the VC dimension and only logarithmic dependence on the robustness parameter, while decoupling sample complexity from the time horizon to make prediction truly everlasting.
limitations: The computationally efficient constructions are limited to axis-aligned rectangles and decision-stumps; the generic PERP construction remains computationally inefficient with sample complexity quadratic in the VC dimension. The paper leaves open whether a generic construction can achieve sample complexity linear in 1/α or sub-linear in 1/γ, and all results are purely theoretical with no empirical validation.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that a simple twist to the privacy definition—requiring δ to be a decreasing function of time rather than a fixed constant—resolves the 'not truly everlasting' problem without inflating sample complexity, which was previously thought to be an inherent limitation of the DP framework. Additionally, the insight that for rectangles one can maintain a single evolving hypothesis (rather than the k independent hypotheses of Naor et al.) to achieve linear-in-dimension sample complexity is a clean structural departure from the prior 'sample and aggregate' paradigm.

title: REGAL: Refactoring Programs to Discover Generalizable Abstractions
task_novelty_note: Program synthesis/induction from queries is well-established; REGAL contributes a new gradient-free refactoring-based method for learning reusable abstractions to aid LLM program prediction.

compares_to.title: Learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as LILO baseline for LOGO with accuracy 41.1, compared against REGAL's 57.1

compares_to.title: Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as Faithful-CoT baseline for Date with accuracy 83.3, compared against REGAL's 90.2

compares_to.title: ReAct: Synergizing reasoning and acting in language models
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as ReAct baseline for TextCraft with accuracy 25.6, compared against REGAL's 30.8

key_contribution: REGAL is a gradient-free method that iteratively refactors a small set of primitive programs into a verified library of reusable helper functions (Code Bank) and usage demonstrations (Demo Bank), enabling LLMs to predict programs more accurately by selecting from learned abstractions rather than reasoning from primitives alone, with a 13B open-source model augmented by REGAL outperforming GPT-3.5 on multiple domains.
limitations: REGAL's code-based abstractions are less flexible than neural-network-parameterized functions in dynamically changing environments (e.g., navigation), and not all domains benefit uniformly—math domains without a clear domain language (MATH, TabMWP) show more modest and inconsistent gains. The method also requires an execution environment for verification, and the learned abstractions are not necessarily the same as those a human programmer would choose.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is that CodeLlama-13B with REGAL abstractions outperforms GPT-3.5 on LOGO (57.1% vs. 49.3%) and TextCraft (26.9% vs. 18.4%), suggesting learned abstractions can partially close the model-size gap. This is supported by consistent improvements across multiple open-source models and ablations, though the effect is weaker on math domains without clear domain languages, tempering the generality claim.

title: RLVF: Learning from Verbal Feedback without Overgeneralization
task_novelty_note: Extends LLM alignment from feedback to the context-dependent setting where feedback applies only to a subset of prompts, rather than universally.

builds_on.title: Direct preference optimization: Your language model is secretly a reward model
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we use the DPO algorithm for learning from preference data in this work' and the C3PO loss directly incorporates L_DPO as its in-scope optimization objective

builds_on.title: A general language assistant as a laboratory for alignment
builds_on.evidence: C3PO uses the SCD/SFT loss formulation (Equation 1) as its regularization term for out-of-scope and near-scope prompts to constrain model behavior change

compares_to.title: A general language assistant as a laboratory for alignment
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as 'SCD' baseline with S_in=0.470, S_out=0.269, S_overall=0.6005

compares_to.title: Direct preference optimization: Your language model is secretly a reward model
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 2 as 'DPO' baseline with S_in=0.326, S_out=0.517, S_overall=0.4045; paper evaluates DPO on in-scope preference data without C3PO's regularization

key_contribution: C3PO, a method that translates a single sentence of verbal feedback into a synthetic preference dataset spanning in-scope, near-scope, and out-of-scope prompts and fine-tunes with a joint DPO + SFT objective, reducing overgeneralization by 30% while maintaining in-scope feedback adherence comparable to in-context prompting, with a theoretical derivation showing the synthetic two-policy preference data satisfies the Bradley-Terry model with a closed-form optimal policy.
limitations: The continual learning evaluation is limited to combining only two feedbacks via LoRA weight mixing, and the relationship between feedback complexity and base model capability remains unexplored. The finding that full KL-divergence distillation is worse than simple SFT for the out-of-scope constraint suggests the optimal constraint formulation is still an open question.
surprise_factor: Two findings stand out: (1) GPT-4 overgeneralizes at a similar rate to Mistral-7B (27% vs 25.4% on near-scope), challenging the assumption that stronger models handle contextual applicability reasoning better; (2) replacing the SFT constraint with full KL-divergence knowledge distillation—a strictly stronger constraint—substantially impairs in-scope adherence, a negative result suggesting that allowing subtle distributional drift on irrelevant prompts is beneficial. Both are well-supported by the 100-feedback evaluation protocol.

title: Causal Inference from Competing Treatments
task_novelty_note: Minimizing causal estimation error under competitive budget allocation with position effects is framed as a new problem absent from both the causal inference and game-theoretic literatures.

builds_on.title: Budget allocation problem with multiple advertisers: A game theoretic view
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Our game-theoretic design is inspired by and directly generalizes the work of Maehara et al. (2015)' and 'We use a probabilistic allocation rule that generalizes the model proposed in Maehara et al. (2015)'

key_contribution: A game-theoretic framework for causal inference under competing treatments that proves a tractable sample value objective (S = Σ n_r·α_r²) approximates the true minimax estimation error objective, with pure Nash equilibria in the sample value game being (ε,η)-approximate equilibria for the error minimization game at rates ε = O(k/√B) and η = O(exp(−B/k²)).
limitations: The analysis assumes known discount factors (α_r), bounded treatment effects (|τ| ≤ 1), and a specific probabilistic allocation rule; the paper is purely theoretical with no empirical validation, and open questions remain regarding the Price of Anarchy, extension to other auction designs (e.g., generalized second-price), and fairness of utility distribution across administrators.
surprise_factor: The main conceptual surprise is that the complex minimax estimation error is well-approximated by a simple weighted sum (sample value S = Σ n_r·α_r²), and that pure Nash equilibria in this tractable proxy game are approximate equilibria for the true error-minimization game with clean rates (ε = O(k/√B), η = O(exp(−B/k²))). The closed-form characterization of equilibria—uniform unit bids, exhaustive budget use, minimal overlap—is also a clean structural result that was not obvious a priori given the probabilistic allocation rule.

title: Online Learning in CMDPs: Handling Stochastic and Adversarial Constraints
task_novelty_note: Extends online learning in CMDPs from stochastic-only constraints to adversarially-selected constraints, a setting explicitly absent from prior work.

builds_on.title: Online convex optimization in adversarial Markov decision processes
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'UC-O-GDPS follows the rationale of the UC-O-REPS algorithm by Rosenberg & Mansour (2019b), from which we highlight two major differences' — the update step is changed from mirror descent to gradient descent to achieve weak no-interval regret.

builds_on.title: The best of many worlds: Dual mirror descent for online allocation problems
builds_on.evidence: Paper states it provides 'the first best-of-both-worlds algorithm for CMDPs with long-term constraints, in the flavor of Balseiro et al. (2023)' — the primal-dual best-of-both-worlds framework is adapted to the CMDP setting.

builds_on.title: A unifying framework for online optimization with long-term constraints
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Differently from previous works on online learning with adversarial constraints, in this work we relax the strong assumption that the algorithm has to know the value of the parameter ρ' which is 'ubiquitous in the adversarily-constrained online optimization literature (see, e.g., (Castiglioni et al., 2022b))' — the framework is extended to remove the need for known ρ.

compares_to.title: Exploration exploitation in constrained mdps
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as a prior work compared on properties: does not handle adversarial rewards or adversarial constraints, but works with unknown ρ and without Slater's condition in MDPs.

compares_to.title: Upper confidence primal-dual reinforcement learning for cmdp with adversarial loss
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as a prior work compared on properties: handles adversarial rewards but not adversarial constraints, works with unknown ρ but requires Slater's condition.

compares_to.title: A unifying framework for online optimization with long-term constraints
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as a prior work compared on properties: handles adversarial rewards and adversarial constraints but requires known ρ, works without Slater's condition, but not in MDPs.

compares_to.title: Provably efficient model-free algorithms for non-stationary cmdps
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 as a prior work compared on properties: does not handle general adversarial rewards or constraints (only bounded non-stationarity), works with unknown ρ but requires Slater's condition.

key_contribution: First best-of-both-worlds algorithm (PDGD-OPS) for online learning in CMDPs that handles both stochastic and adversarial rewards and constraints without requiring knowledge of the Slater parameter ρ, achieving Õ(√T) regret and constraint violation under Slater's condition, Õ(T^{3/4}) otherwise, and no-α-regret (α = ρ/(1+ρ)) under adversarial constraints, via a novel weak no-interval regret property that automatically bounds dual variables.
limitations: The analysis is restricted to loop-free episodic CMDPs with full-information feedback (the entire reward vector and constraint matrix are revealed after each episode), and the paper provides purely theoretical guarantees with no empirical validation. The T^{3/4} bound in the degenerate regime (small ρ) may not be tight, and the loop-free assumption, while castable from general episodic MDPs, requires duplicating the state space L times.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that the weak no-interval regret property (never previously studied in episodic adversarial MDPs) is the key technical ingredient that automatically bounds dual variables, eliminating the need to know ρ — a property that standard no-regret guarantees are insufficient to provide. Additionally, the paper notes the counter-intuitive result that adversarial rewards yield a tighter regret bound than stochastic rewards, due to the different optimization baselines used in each setting.

title: Designing Decision Support Systems using Counterfactual Prediction Sets
task_novelty_note: Finding the optimal conformal predictor for a prediction-set-based decision support system was defined by Straitouri et al. (2023); this paper provides a new online, assumption-free algorithm to solve it.

builds_on.title: Algorithmic Learning in a Random World
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we favor conformal predictors over alternatives for two key reasons. First, they provide prediction sets with a nested structure that, together with the counterfactual monotonicity assumption, will allow us to find the optimal conformal predictor that maximizes the average accuracy of the expert's predictions very efficiently.'

builds_on.title: Conformal prediction: A gentle introduction
builds_on.venue: Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 2023
builds_on.evidence: Cited alongside Vovk et al. (2005) as the foundational conformal prediction framework whose nested prediction set structure and PAC coverage guarantees the algorithm relies on.

builds_on.title: Introduction to multi-armed bandits
builds_on.venue: Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning 2019
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'a variant of the successive elimination algorithm (Slivkins, 2019), which we refer to as counterfactual successive elimination, achieves an exponential improvement in regret in comparison with vanilla successive elimination.' Also adapts UCB1 from this bandit framework.

builds_on.title: Improving expert predictions with conformal prediction
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Straitouri et al. (2023) have argued that an alternative type of decision support systems may provide such a guarantee' and 'our goal is to lift this assumption and efficiently find the optimal conformal predictor that maximizes the average accuracy achieved by real experts.' The paper directly extends this work by removing the stylized expert model assumption.

compares_to.title: Improving expert predictions with conformal prediction
compares_to.evidence: Figure 3 annotates 'the α values found by the algorithms by Straitouri et al. (2023) [1]' and the paper states 'the conformal predictor found by our counterfactual successive elimination algorithm offers greater performance than that found by the algorithm by Straitouri et al. (2023), which uses a stylized expert model.'

compares_to.title: On the utility of prediction sets in human-ai teams
compares_to.evidence: Figure 3 annotates 'the α value used by Babbar et al. (2022) [2]' for the lenient implementation, and the paper compares strict vs. lenient implementations where the lenient one follows Babbar et al.'s approach.

key_contribution: An assumption-free online learning methodology that exploits the nested structure of conformal prediction sets and a counterfactual monotonicity assumption to efficiently find the optimal conformal predictor for decision support systems, achieving an exponential regret improvement over vanilla bandit algorithms and demonstrating through a large-scale human study (n=2,751) that restricting experts' agency to prediction sets outperforms allowing full agency.
limitations: Evaluation is limited to a single image classification benchmark (ImageNet16H) with non-domain experts, raising questions about generalizability to other tasks and high-stakes domains. The counterfactual monotonicity assumption cannot be directly validated (it sits at level 3 of Pearl's causal ladder), and the framework does not account for fairness considerations, distribution shift, or label noise.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is a conceptual surprise: the strict implementation, which forces experts to choose only from the prediction set, consistently outperforms the lenient implementation that allows experts to pick any label — contradicting the intuitive expectation that more agency yields better performance. This is well-evidenced (n=2,751, 194,407 predictions) but demonstrated on a single dataset and task type, so generalizability remains uncertain.

title: DéjàVu: KV-cache Streaming for Fast, Fault-tolerant Generative LLM Serving
task_novelty_note: Distributed LLM inference serving is a well-established task; the paper contributes new system-level techniques (disaggregation, swapping, replication) rather than a new problem formulation.

builds_on.title: NVIDIA FasterTransformer
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'DéjàVu is built on top of FasterTransformer, supporting both tensor and pipeline parallelism' and uses its KV cache preallocation and pipeline parallelism infrastructure as the foundation.

compares_to.title: NVIDIA FasterTransformer
compares_to.evidence: Paper states 'We compare DéjàVu with FasterTransformer, as it supports pipeline parallelism for LLM inference' and FasterTransformer (modified) appears as the baseline in Figures 8, 9, 10, 11, and Appendix B tables with direct numerical comparisons on throughput, latency, and makespan.

key_contribution: DéjàVu introduces DéjàVuLib, a modular KV cache streaming library that underpins three system-level optimizations for pipeline-parallel LLM serving—prompt-token disaggregation with a closed-form resource allocator, microbatch-level GPU-CPU cache swapping, and ring-based KV cache replication for fault tolerance—achieving up to 2× throughput improvement and 1.54× faster failure recovery over FasterTransformer.
limitations: End-to-end evaluation is limited to small clusters (2–4 machines with 2 GPUs each) and a narrow set of models (GPT2, OPT, BLOOM), with the planner simulation (Appendix B) used to extrapolate to larger deployments due to budget constraints. The paper acknowledges that disaggregation requires at least ~20 Gbps network bandwidth to be beneficial, and that integration with TensorRT-LLM and dynamic reconfiguration under shifting workloads remain future work.
surprise_factor: The 95× speedup from buffered copies in DéjàVuLib is a notable engineering result, showing that the naive approach of issuing many small cudaMemcpy calls is catastrophically inefficient for KV cache streaming. The planner simulation revealing that DéjàVu's makespan advantage *grows* with cluster size (4.2× over baseline at 16 machines) is a useful scaling insight, though the end-to-end evaluation on real hardware is limited to 4–8 machines, tempering confidence in extrapolation to much larger deployments.

title: Learning from Streaming Data when Users Choose
task_novelty_note: Extends multi-learner retraining under user choice from full-information batched retraining to streaming single-sample updates with non-stationary induced distributions.

builds_on.title: Emergent specialization from participation dynamics and multi-learner retraining
builds_on.evidence: Paper extends Dean et al.'s full-information multi-learner retraining setting to streaming data, stating 'a property that Dean et al. (2024) leveraged to prove convergence in the full information setting' and that prior work 'does not adequately handle the realistic setting in which user data is sampled from the population and arrives in a streaming manner.'

builds_on.title: Competing AI: How does competition feedback affect machine learning?
builds_on.evidence: Paper states these works 'form a conceptual foundation for our paper' regarding the coupled dynamics of user choice and model retraining, extending their framework to streaming data with bounded rationality.

builds_on.title: Convergence of online k-means
builds_on.evidence: Paper directly uses So et al.'s directional derivative technique to compute the gradient of f_PR(Θ), stating 'Similar to So et al. (2022), we decouple the difference f_PR(Θ+γv)−f_PR(Θ) into two parts' and notes their work 'share[s] similar structure to the specialization that results from MSGD.'

builds_on.title: Performative prediction
builds_on.evidence: Paper's learning objective is derived from performative prediction, stating 'This objective can be understood as minimizing the loss of the distribution induced by the parameters, similar to the notion of performative optimality introduced by Perdomo et al. (2020).'

key_contribution: Formalizes the dynamics of streaming users choosing among competing service providers with bounded rationality, proposes MSGD—a simple decentralized algorithm where each service performs a single gradient step on the one data point it receives—and proves almost-sure convergence to stationary points of the overall social-welfare loss by connecting streaming data and user choice to induced sub-populations.
limitations: The theoretical convergence guarantee is limited to the bounded-rationality user model (random choice with probability ζ); the Boltzmann-rational model is only empirically validated without theoretical analysis. The learning objective is restricted to overall user loss (social welfare), and alternative objectives such as market share, population-level fairness, or explicit competition/coordination mechanisms are left as future work.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that a trivially simple algorithm—just one SGD step on the single data point received—converges to stationary points of a non-convex, non-stationary objective despite the update not being risk-reducing (no monotonic decrease in f(Θ) is guaranteed). The empirical finding that less data (MSGD) outperforms more data (full information) when users are rational is counterintuitive but well-motivated by the specialization mechanism.

key_contribution: AURA (AUROC Adaptation), a hyperparameter-free neural intervention that dampens toxicity expert neuron activations proportionally to their AUROC-based expertise, achieving up to 2.2× toxicity reduction with only 0.72 perplexity increase across LLMs from 1.5B to 40B parameters while preserving zero-shot common-sense reasoning.
limitations: The method is validated only for toxicity mitigation (not other harmful concepts), considers only linear layers outside attention blocks, and is a static intervention that cannot be dynamically toggled for specific contexts. Its effectiveness is contingent on the quality of the labeled dataset used to rank experts and on the model's ability to encode the target concept in identifiable neurons.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is that a simple Gini-coefficient-based proportional dampening (AURA) matches the best tuned DAMP configuration (requiring sweeps over k and α) without any hyperparameters, and that it robustly counteracts adversarial pre-prompts—returning toxicity below the unmodified model's level in most cases. The architecture-dependent behavior (Det_zero outperforming AURA on SwiGLU models like Mistral and Llama-v2) is an intriguing open observation rather than a resolved surprise.

title: Networked Inequality: Preferential Attachment Bias in Graph Neural Network Link Prediction
task_novelty_note: Extends fair link prediction from dyadic (inter-group vs. intra-group) fairness to within-group fairness among subgroups within a single social group.

builds_on.title: Semi-supervised classification with graph convolutional networks
builds_on.evidence: The paper's entire theoretical analysis and fairness regularizer are derived for and applied to GCNs with symmetric and random walk normalized filters; the method would not exist without this architecture.

builds_on.title: Representation learning on graphs with jumping knowledge networks
builds_on.evidence: Lemma 4.1 explicitly states 'Similarly to Xu et al. (2018)' and adopts their path activation probability assumption; Theorem 4.3 follows 'a relaxed assumption from Xu et al. (2018)'. The Taylor expansion and expected representation framework is directly derived from this work.

builds_on.title: Fairness-aware learning through regularization approach
builds_on.evidence: The paper states 'we can add a fairness regularization term L_fair to our original GNN training loss (Kamishima et al., 2011)', directly adapting their regularization-based fairness approach to the GNN link prediction setting.

key_contribution: Proves via spectral graph theory that GCNs with a symmetric normalized filter exhibit a within-group preferential attachment bias in link prediction (scores proportional to the geometric mean of within-group degrees), and proposes a new within-group fairness metric and a simple training-time regularizer to mitigate the resulting 'rich get richer' amplification of degree and power disparities among social subgroups.
limitations: The theoretical analysis is restricted to GCNs with an inner-product score function (though Hadamard+MLP is tested empirically), and the random walk filter theory predicts no PA bias yet experiments show moderate degree dependence, indicating a gap between theory and practice. The fairness regularizer requires model retraining and is not applicable to frozen or post-hoc settings, and the authors note the approach is not a 'silver bullet' for addressing all forms of networked inequality.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that a standard, unmodified GCN with a symmetric normalized filter inherently encodes a preferential attachment bias in its link prediction scores—proportional to the geometric mean of within-group degrees—without any explicit degree-based feature, meaning widely-deployed recommender systems may be silently amplifying social inequalities. The empirical gap for the random walk filter (theory predicts no PA bias, but experiments show moderate association) is a secondary but interesting finding.

key_contribution: Proving that the constrained binary integer linear program for RNA secondary structure post-processing is equivalent to a Linear Sum Assignment Problem, enabling an exact O(L³) solution via the Jonker-Volgenant algorithm that guarantees zero constraint violations while outperforming existing post-processing methods in both predictive accuracy and runtime.
limitations: The two-stage architecture disconnects the computational graph, preventing end-to-end training where the backbone network could learn to anticipate the post-processing step. Additionally, the O(L³) assignment solver may be prohibitive for very long RNA sequences (tens of thousands of nucleotides), though approximate faster algorithms could serve as alternatives at the cost of optimality.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is a negative-result surprise: widely adopted post-processing methods (E2Efold's gradient-based solver, REDfold's argmax, Blossom matching) were assumed to enforce structural constraints but actually produce constraint-violating outputs in 56–58% of cases for the overlap constraint (C4). The fix itself—recasting the problem as an assignment problem—is a natural and well-known technique, so the conceptual surprise is moderate.

key_contribution: Proposes RCPO, the first robust constrained policy optimization algorithm applicable to continuous state spaces, featuring a novel robust performance difference lemma and a two-step (improvement + projection) update that provides per-iteration theoretical guarantees on worst-case reward improvement and constraint violation under model mismatch.
limitations: The algorithm requires a known or estimable (s,a)-rectangular uncertainty set of transition kernels, and the worst-case kernel must be estimated via iterative projected gradient descent at each policy update, adding significant computational overhead. The paper does not provide an explicit limitations section, but the evaluation is limited to four relatively simple environments (gambler, N-chain, frozen-lake, point gather) and a single constraint, and the constraint violation bound depends on a ratio of visitation distributions that may be large in practice.
surprise_factor: The main conceptual contribution—the robust performance difference lemma showing that the surrogate approximation (using the current policy's worst-case kernel) still yields guaranteed improvement—is a clean but expected extension of the non-robust result. The empirical results (RCPO satisfying constraints while all baselines violate them) are consistent with the algorithm design rather than surprising. No particularly surprising findings; the contribution is a well-executed theoretical extension with matching experiments.

key_contribution: Introduces DFA-RAG, a framework that learns a Deterministic Finite Automaton from training dialogues to serve as an interpretable semantic router for retrieval-augmented generation, achieving ~4% win-rate improvement over standard RAG and 90.0% Success on MultiWOZ without ground-truth dialogue states, while remaining plug-and-play compatible with any pre-trained LLM.
limitations: The OOD handling strategy (falling back to the last valid DFA state) is heuristic rather than principled, and the framework assumes a coherent multi-turn workflow is embedded in the training data, limiting applicability to open-domain or highly branching conversational settings. Integration with external tools (e.g., web search) for out-of-DFA queries is identified as future work rather than implemented.
surprise_factor: No particularly surprising findings — the ~4% win-rate improvement over RAG is modest and the competitive MultiWOZ scores (93.3 Inform / 90.0 Success without ground-truth states) are reasonable given the structured retrieval. The conceptual elegance of a learned DFA as a semantic router is appealing, but the empirical gains do not dramatically exceed what a well-tuned RAG baseline achieves.

builds_on.evidence: The protection function-based algorithm (PFA) structure and optimal worst-case protection function are derived from this work: 'PFA can optimally solve the one-way trading problem when the protection function is given by...'

compares_to.evidence: WOA (worst-case optimal randomized algorithm, e/(e-1)-competitive) appears in Figure 1 as a baseline compared against the proposed algorithms

key_contribution: Introduces a distributionally-robust competitive ratio (DRCR) as a design objective for online algorithms augmented with uncertainty-quantified predictions, and provides two complementary paradigms—an optimization-based approach yielding optimal algorithms for ski rental and online search, and an ε-net-based online learning approach achieving sublinear policy regret in multi-instance settings—both leveraging probabilistic interval predictions from conformal inference.
limitations: The framework is demonstrated only on two classic problems (ski rental and online search) and is restricted to probabilistic interval predictions as the UQ form; the paper acknowledges that for general UQ forms where tractable ambiguity sets cannot be constructed, the online learning approach relies on Lipschitzness conditions that may not hold broadly, and the empirical evaluation is limited to ski rental.
surprise_factor: A modest conceptual surprise: the straightforward meta-algorithm (tuning the hyperparameter of existing consistent/robust algorithms to minimize the DRCR) completely fails to extract any benefit from low-quality predictions (δ > 1/2), while the new DSR algorithm still improves over worst-case by explicitly using the prediction value in the decision rule. This shows that UQ information cannot be exploited merely through parameter selection but requires structural changes to the algorithm's decision logic.

key_contribution: Formulates a differentiable structural information (DSI) objective that enables deep graph clustering without a predefined cluster number K, and implements it via LSEnet, a neural network in the Lorentz model of hyperbolic space that learns a partitioning tree bottom-up using Lorentz convolution and a closed-form geometric centroid, achieving state-of-the-art clustering on Cora, Citeseer, and Computer benchmarks.
limitations: The method requires setting the tree height H and per-level node counts N_h as hyperparameters, and evaluation is limited to relatively small graphs (up to ~13.7k nodes), leaving scalability to large-scale graphs unverified. The paper does not include an explicit limitations section, but the need for a 'large enough' N_h at each level and the sensitivity to H (Fig. 3) suggest practical tuning overhead.
surprise_factor: No particularly surprising findings — the performance gains over strong baselines are modest (1–3% NMI/ARI on most datasets), and the hyperbolic-space choice is well-motivated by the tree-embedding theorem. The >20% NMI gain over RGC on AMAP is notable but compares against a fundamentally different (RL-based) method rather than a like-for-like structural-entropy baseline.

title: Online Adaptive Anomaly Thresholding with Confidence Sequences
task_novelty_note: Extends online anomaly thresholding (existing in DSpot, Siffer et al.) by adding distribution-free guarantees, shift adaptivity, and offline-data integration in a unified framework.

builds_on.evidence: The paper states 'Theorem 1 (Theorem 2 from (Howard and Ramdas, 2022))' and directly uses their confidence sequence construction for quantiles as the core mechanism of the thresholding algorithm.
