key_contribution: A computationally efficient sliced Wasserstein distance for spherical probability measures (S3W) that composes stereographic projection with an injective nearly-isometric correction function and the Radon transform to reduce spherical OT to 1D linear OT on the real line, achieving up to 20× speedup over prior spherical sliced methods while maintaining competitive accuracy, along with a rotationally invariant variant (RI-S3W/ARI-S3W) and proof that the method defines a valid metric on P_p(S^d).
limitations: The method requires a fixed projection point (north pole) and handles the resulting singularity via an ε-cap, and the rotationally invariant variant incurs a multiplicative cost proportional to the number of rotations N_R. The paper does not address unbalanced or partial transport settings on the sphere, and the ε-cap introduces a small approximation that may affect accuracy for distributions with significant mass near the projection point.
surprise_factor: No particularly surprising findings — the speed advantage is well-motivated by the algorithmic difference between 1D linear OT and circular OT, and the accuracy results are competitive but not dramatically better than SSW. The clean reduction of spherical sliced OT to a stereographic-projection-plus-Radon-transform pipeline is elegant but follows naturally from the existing GRT framework.

title: Inferring the Long-Term Causal Effects of Long-Term Treatments from Short-Term Experiments
input: short-term experimental data (s, a, y, s' tuples)
task_novelty_note: Extends long-term causal inference from short-term data (surrogate methods) to the harder sub-case of continual-exposure treatments where mediation fails by definition.

builds_on.title: Efficiently breaking the curse of horizon in off-policy evaluation with double reinforcement learning
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We make direct use of an estimator from (Kallus & Uehara, 2022) that combines two functions: the Q function... and the density ratio function' and the entire doubly-robust estimator in Section 3 is derived from this work.

builds_on.title: Minimax weight and q-function learning for off-policy evaluation
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'For the density ratio functions, we use the Minimax weight estimator from (Uehara et al., 2020)' and the density ratio estimation in Section 3.4 directly implements the Minimax formulation from this paper.

builds_on.title: Breaking the curse of horizon: Infinite-horizon off-policy estimation
builds_on.evidence: Paper attributes the density ratio function concept to this work: 'the density ratio function (Liu et al., 2018; Uehara et al., 2020)' as a core component of the estimator.

compares_to.title: Combining experimental and observational data to estimate treatment effects on long term outcomes
compares_to.evidence: Surrogate index method is directly compared in Figure 3 (Simple MDP) and Figure 6 (Sepsis Simulator) alongside the proposed ORL method, with the paper showing it 'implicitly estimates a truncated effect' for long-term treatments.

key_contribution: Reframes the estimation of long-term causal effects of continual-exposure treatments from short-term experiments as an off-policy evaluation problem in a Markov Decision Process, constructing equivalent stationary stochastic policies for arbitrary-duration treatments and developing a doubly-robust, asymptotically efficient estimator based on Q-function and density-ratio function estimation that eliminates the need for surrogacy assumptions.
limitations: All empirical validation is on simulated data (a simple MDP and a sepsis simulator) with no real-world application, and the method's accuracy depends critically on the state space being sufficiently rich to satisfy the Markov property—the hidden-state experiment shows severe downward bias when unobserved states drive reward dynamics. Additionally, the stationary-policy approximation used to make the Q function tractable degrades in quality for shorter treatment durations, and the overlap condition is stronger than standard causal inference settings, requiring treatment rollout across the entire state space.
surprise_factor: The conceptual finding that surrogate index methods, even when all their assumptions hold, implicitly estimate only a truncated treatment effect (active only up to the surrogate measurement time) for long-term treatments is a useful and somewhat unexpected clarification of a widely-used methodology's blind spot. However, the method itself is a fairly direct application of existing doubly-robust off-policy evaluation tools, and the empirical validation is limited to simulated data (a simple MDP and a sepsis simulator), so the practical impact remains to be demonstrated on real-world long-term treatment settings.

title: Agent-Specific Effects: A Causal Effect Propagation Analysis in Multi-Agent MDPs
task_novelty_note: Authors explicitly state this is the first work studying causal effect propagation through specific agents in multi-agent sequential decision making; path-specific effects measure path-based, not agent-based, propagation.

builds_on.title: Direct and indirect effects
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we define the notion of fixed path-specific effects (FPSE) utilizing a similar path-deactivation process as in Definition 6.1' and establishes a formal connection via Lemma 6.3 showing ASE equals FPSE

builds_on.title: Nested counterfactual identification from arbitrary surrogate experiments
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Our proof leverages a novel identification formula, Eq. (2), that allows us to express counterfactual factors (Correa et al., 2021) in terms of the observational distribution'

builds_on.title: Woulda, coulda, shoulda: Counterfactually-guided policy search
builds_on.evidence: Paper states '(Buesing et al., 2018) shows that such parameterization of a partially observable MDP to an SCM is always possible. Their result can be directly extended to MMDPs'

compares_to.title: Direct and indirect effects
compares_to.evidence: cf-PSE (counterfactual path-specific effect from Pearl 2001) is computed alongside cf-ASE in Figures 4c, 4d and 5a-5d; paper states 'Compared to cf-ASE, we observe that cf-PSE suggests a less prominent pattern for the clinician-specific effect'

key_contribution: Introduces agent-specific effects (ASE) and counterfactual ASE (cf-ASE), a novel causal quantity for multi-agent MDPs that measures the effect of an agent's action on the outcome through a selected subset of agents, proves identifiability under the weaker noise monotonicity assumption (rather than model bijectiveness), provides an unbiased sampling-based estimation algorithm, and establishes a formal connection to path-specific effects via a new generalized notion (fixed path-specific effects).
limitations: The identifiability results require the noise monotonicity assumption, which is restrictive and often violated in practice; experiments are limited to simulation-based environments (Graph and Sepsis) without access to the true underlying causal model. The paper does not address identifiability in the presence of unobserved confounding, nor does it provide a causal explanation formula for decomposing effects across individual agents and environment states.
surprise_factor: The conceptual distinction between cf-ASE and cf-PSE is the most notable finding: cf-PSE can assign positive effect values when the clinician never overrides the AI (counter-intuitive), while cf-ASE correctly yields zero, revealing that the standard path-specific framework has a structural blind spot in multi-agent settings. The experimental observation that ~40% of high-TCFE AI actions also have high clinician-specific effect is practically interesting but based on a single simulation environment with restrictive assumptions.

key_contribution: A subgraph-based diffusion framework (SGDM) that converts single-graph training into learning over sampled subgraphs with global positional context, enabling three new conditional editing tasks—denoising, expansion, and style transfer—on a single partially observable network while making previously infeasible GDDM backbones (e.g., DiGRESS) scalable to large-scale graphs.
limitations: The authors explicitly state that future work will expand evaluation to include downstream task performance and support for editing dynamic graphs. In practice, the expansion task shows near-zero consensus across all backbones, and the evaluation is limited to three datasets with only 10 generated samples per metric, leaving open questions about scalability to truly production-scale networks.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is a negative result: the expansion task essentially fails for all methods (consensus ≈ 0, diversity ≈ 0.1), suggesting that recovering missing edges via diffusion-based in-painting is far harder than denoising. Additionally, global context (LPEs) unexpectedly degrades triangle-count style transfer (MAE doubles from ~9 to ~19.6), hinting that positional encodings encode structural information that conflicts with certain topological edits. However, these findings are based on only 3 datasets and 10 samples, limiting their generality.

key_contribution: QuIP# achieves state-of-the-art post-training quantization of LLMs at ≤4 bits per weight by combining Randomized Hadamard Transform incoherence processing, a hardware-efficient E8 lattice-based vector quantization codebook (E8P), and inter-layer fine-tuning, demonstrating for the first time that 3-bit quantized models can outperform 4-bit models.
limitations: The fine-tuning step, while cheap relative to QAT, still requires ~50–100 GPU-hours for a 70B model and the authors note their fine-tuning and multi-codebook (RVQ) approaches are 'almost certainly not optimal.' Additionally, the RHT requires dimensions to factor into known Hadamard matrix sizes (falling back to the slightly weaker RFFT otherwise), and the fast-inference design constraints on the codebook may sacrifice some quantization quality compared to unconstrained alternatives.
surprise_factor: The most striking result is conceptual: 3-bit QuIP# consistently outperforms 4-bit QuIP# across Llama 1 and 2 at 7B, 13B, and 70B, and even beats a theoretical lossless 4-bit model on Llama 2 — directly contradicting the '4-bit is optimal' scaling-law claim of Dettmers & Zettlemoyer (2023). This is well-evidenced (multiple model sizes, two model families, two perplexity datasets, and zeroshot tasks), making it a genuine paradigm shift rather than a cherry-picked number. A secondary surprise is that the structured E8P codebook empirically outperforms a K-means codebook fitted to the actual (Gaussian) source distribution, suggesting that packing density and symmetry matter more than distributional matching in practice.

key_contribution: Proposes PLOT, an indirect online tracking algorithm that learns time-varying autoregressive target dynamics via RLS with exponential forgetting and applies them in certainty-equivalent receding horizon control, achieving dynamic regret O(√(TV_T)) where V_T is the total variation of the target dynamics (yielding logarithmic regret for structured targets like circular motion), validated on a real Crazyflie quadrotor.
limitations: The regret guarantees assume the target is exactly realizable by the AR model with bounded dynamics; it is open whether guarantees extend to non-realizable targets, output tracking, or non-quadratic costs. Additionally, the tuning rule in Corollary 4.2 requires knowledge of the path length V_T, which is not always available in practice, and the hardware validation uses a linearized quadrotor model.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that the right complexity measure for structured targets is the variation of the dynamics matrix S_t (zero for circular/constant-velocity targets) rather than the target state r_t (linear in T), which flips the regret from O(T) to O(log T) for common tracking scenarios. This is a clean theoretical insight rather than an empirical shock, and the hardware validation, while notable as a first, uses a simple linearized model.

title: Overcoming the Optimizer's Curse Obtaining Realistic Prescriptions from Neural Networks
task_novelty_note: Extends the established task of optimizing over trained neural networks by adding a certified realism constraint (LOF-based) to the decision space.

builds_on.title: Deep neural networks and mixed integer linear optimization

builds_on.title: LOF: Identifying density-based local outliers
builds_on.evidence: The paper's core contribution is reformulating the LOF metric as a single tractable optimization constraint; without LOF the realism constraint and the entire adaptive sampling algorithm would not exist.

builds_on.title: Manifold-aligned counterfactual explanations for neural networks

builds_on.title: Bounding and counting linear regions of deep neural networks
builds_on.evidence: The proof of Proposition 4.6 directly invokes this result: 'By invoking the result of Serra et al. (2018), N is upper bounded by' the combinatorial expression, which is essential to the sample complexity guarantee.

key_contribution: Reformulates the Local Outlier Factor (LOF) metric as a single tractable linear or quadratic constraint to enforce realism in neural network optimization, and proposes an adaptive sampling algorithm that partitions the decision space into realistic polytopes, reducing one intractable MIP into a small number of easy LP/SOCP subproblems to obtain certified realistic prescriptions from ReLU networks and general differentiable models.
limitations: The method is post-hoc (optimization over a fixed trained network) rather than integrated into end-to-end training, and for general differentiable models the projected gradient ascent step only guarantees convergence to local optima. The k=1 LOF constraint and the user-defined threshold t may be insufficient or poorly calibrated in very high-dimensional spaces, and the adaptive sampling, while bounded by |D|, is stochastic and does not guarantee the global optimum in a single run.
surprise_factor: The most notable result is the dramatic scalability gap: the MIP baseline fails entirely (NA) on all networks beyond 3×100 within 60 seconds, while the proposed method handles 9-layer networks with millions of parameters in the same window, and the Theorem 4.3.2 upper bound prunes 87.5–99.9% of realistic polytopes. This is conceptually satisfying but follows logically from the geometric argument, so it is more a strong confirmation of the theory than a genuine surprise.

limitations: The evaluation is limited to two transformer-based backbones (TimesNet and Autoformer) and Gaussian predictive distributions with diagonal covariance; the Lagrange multiplier for the general oblique projection is fixed at 10^4 rather than being adaptive, and scalability beyond the largest tested hierarchy (76,304 bottom-level series in TourismLarge) is not explored.
surprise_factor: No particularly surprising findings — the learnable oblique projections (GenProj, Eucl) consistently but modestly outperform the fixed orthogonal projection (Hier-E2E) and sequential MinT baselines across all five datasets and both backbones, with typical RMSE improvements of 3–8%. The spectral norm analysis showing that harder datasets yield projections farther from orthogonal is an intuitive but nicely quantified observation rather than a genuine surprise.

key_contribution: First proof of simplicity bias and precise mathematical characterization of learned features for general non-linearly-separable datasets in two-layer networks trained from small initialization, showing that prominent neurons cluster around global extrema of a width-independent data-dependent function G, and that extreme simplicity bias intensifies in the infinite-time limit for XOR-like data.
limitations: Results are restricted to two-layer networks and the small-initialization regime; the extreme simplicity bias characterization for XOR-like data relies on an assumption about 4-neuron convergence (Assumption 5.4) that is only empirically validated rather than proven, and the even-dimension case is left open. Empirical validation is limited to a single dataset (MNIST-CIFAR10 domino) and a single architecture (ResNet-18).
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that simplicity bias not only persists but intensifies in the infinite-time limit for non-linearly-separable data, causing the network to effectively 'forget' all features except the simplest ones — a mechanism that explains why longer training can hurt OOD transfer. The empirical confirmation (8.13% OOD accuracy drop, p≈10⁻⁶) is supported by a single dataset and architecture, so the evidence is suggestive but not yet broadly validated.

title: Exploration by Optimization with Hybrid Regularizers: Logarithmic Regret with Adversarial Robustness in Partial Monitoring
task_novelty_note: BOBW in partial monitoring was established by Tsuchiya et al. (2023a); this paper improves the regret bounds for the same task.

key_contribution: Introduces a hybrid regularizer (log-barrier + complement negative Shannon entropy) into the exploration-by-optimization framework for partial monitoring, with a new analysis over a k-independent feasible region, achieving the first O(log T) stochastic regret bounds for best-of-both-worlds algorithms in both locally and globally observable games — a Θ(k² log T) improvement over prior BOBW bounds.
limitations: The paper explicitly notes that little is understood about the true minimax dependencies on k, d, and m, and investigating these is left as future work. Additionally, the globally observable game bound carries a k-times worse dependence on k compared to the locally observable case, and the analysis assumes non-degenerate games with no duplicate actions.
surprise_factor: The Θ(k² log T) improvement in the stochastic bound is substantial but largely anticipated given the known log²T limitation of Shannon entropy regularizers and the known O(log T) properties of log-barrier regularizers in simpler settings. The more interesting conceptual point is that the hybrid regularizer cannot be naively plugged into ExO for PM — the existing analysis relies heavily on Shannon entropy properties, and the new feasible region R(q) plus water-transfer-based bounding of the stability term without uniform mixing was a non-obvious technical hurdle. No genuinely surprising negative or positive result; the improvements are well-motivated and follow from known regularizer properties.

key_contribution: Comprehensive empirical study of 35 VLMs demonstrating that temperature scaling achieves robust calibration (ECE ~0.05) across distribution shifts, different label sets, semantic hierarchy levels, and with as few as 40–50 calibration images, and that synthetic images generated by GPT-3 + Stable Diffusion can serve as effective calibration sets when labeled data is unavailable.
limitations: The study is restricted to classification confidence calibration for backbone VLMs (e.g., CLIP, BLIP) and does not extend to regression confidence estimates, LLM-based VLMs (e.g., LLaVA), or compound architectures for tasks such as object detection and segmentation.
surprise_factor: The most striking finding is the extreme data efficiency: VLMs reach near-optimal calibration with only 40–50 images even on 1000-way ImageNet, and a single generic prompt ('a photo of a <class>') suffices for calibration that transfers to other prompt sets. This challenges the working assumption that reliable calibration requires domain-matched, label-aligned, and sufficiently large calibration sets — a conceptual surprise well-supported across 35 models, multiple OOD benchmarks, and four calibration methods.

title: Coactive Learning for Large Language Models using Implicit User Feedback
task_novelty_note: Extends LLM alignment from preference feedback (RLHF) to a new implicit-edit feedback modality, replacing explicit dueling comparisons with user-generated improvements.

builds_on.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023), which we will employ in CoRLL' and uses DPO as the core policy update in Algorithm 2 line 8

builds_on.title: Coactive Learning
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'This theorem generalizes the results of Shivaswamy & Joachims (2015) to general pairwise preference learners' and derives the theoretical framework from this work

compares_to.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
compares_to.evidence: Compared as 'Dueling' baseline in Figures 3, 7, 9, and 10 where DPO is applied with dueling feedback instead of coactive feedback; paper states 'We use the same DPO pairwise preference learner for dueling as for CoRLL'

key_contribution: Introduces coactive learning as a framework for training LLMs from implicit user edit feedback, derives the first regret bound for non-linear coactive models (Theorem 3.1), and proposes CoRLL—the first coactive learning algorithm for LLMs—which outperforms noise-free dueling RLHF on summarization and helpfulness tasks even with weak or ~40% noisy feedback.
limitations: All coactive feedback is simulated by an expert policy rather than collected from real human users, leaving open whether the approach generalizes to the messier, less consistent edits real users produce. The large-scale experiments use k=1 for argmax approximation due to compute constraints, and the paper acknowledges that better argmax approximations and alternative pairwise preference learners remain open design questions.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is that minimally informative coactive feedback (even just editing the last 5 tokens) achieves a better reward-KL tradeoff than noise-free dueling feedback, which challenges the assumption that explicit pairwise comparisons are the most data-efficient preference signal. However, this result is based on simulated feedback from a single expert policy across three tasks, so the practical generality remains uncertain.

key_contribution: A two-stage self-learning framework for dialog ASR that combines explicit audio/text context modeling, implicit context learning via PF-CLC contrastive loss augmented by a novel online hard-negative mining algorithm (Ohm), and student-teacher distillation to transfer context-awareness into a context-free streaming model, achieving up to 26% relative WER reduction on OD3 and ~10% on real-world dialog data.
limitations: The paper acknowledges negative transfer on low-diversity domains (e.g., home automation, -22.68% WERR) where context over-reliance degrades performance, and identifies dynamic context gating as future work. Additionally, the real-world evaluation relies on closed-source data and the OD3 results are on semi-synthetic data, limiting full reproducibility and generalizability claims.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is that a 200M context-trained teacher outperforms a 1B non-context model, and that context knowledge distilled into a context-free student retains meaningful gains (~4% WERR) — suggesting training-time context is a more parameter-efficient path than scaling. The negative result on home automation (context hurts when disambiguation is unnecessary) is an honest and useful observation, though the overall improvements (~10% real-world, 26% OD3) are solid but not paradigm-shifting given the combination of known techniques.

key_contribution: A hybrid asynchronous-to-synchronous pipeline (ALERT-Transformer) that enables event-by-event processing of sparse event-based vision data within standard dense ML frameworks, using a PointNet-based embedding with sinusoidal time encoding and Old Maximum Value Decay to achieve state-of-the-art gesture recognition at 9.6 ms latency without modifying the underlying PointNet architecture.
limitations: Validation is limited to two classification tasks (gesture recognition and binary car detection) with a Transformer backbone; the authors note that applicability to other architectures (CNNs), other tasks (segmentation, detection, generative), and hardware deployment remain open. The accuracy gap versus frame-based state-of-the-art (84.6% SA vs. 97.9% NVA) is significant for ultra-low-latency operation, and the LMM variant drops to 72.9% SA.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is conceptual rather than numerical: keeping the PointNet architecture completely unaltered (preserving AI-accelerator compatibility) while achieving asynchronous processing through a simple exponential decay at the token level is a clean architectural insight. The ablation showing accuracy collapses to 25.9% without OMVD confirms the decay is not a minor tweak but a load-bearing component. The 0.4% accuracy cost of sinusoidal time encoding for bounded continuous time is also pleasantly low, though the overall accuracy gap versus frame-based SOTA (84.6% vs. 97.9%) tempers the excitement.

title: Matroid Semi-Bandits in Sublinear Time
task_novelty_note: Matroid semi-bandits are a well-studied task; the contribution is a faster algorithm for the same problem.

builds_on.title: Matroid bandits: Fast combinatorial optimization with learning
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'The design of FasterCUCB is based on CUCB, but with a much faster sampling rule which takes time sublinear in K'

compares_to.title: Matroid bandits: Fast combinatorial optimization with learning
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 alongside FasterCUCB with per-round time complexity comparison for uniform, partition, graphical, and transversal matroids

key_contribution: The first sublinear-time algorithm (FasterCUCB) for matroid semi-bandits, achieving per-round complexity of O(D·polylog(K)·polylog(T)) for uniform, partition, and graphical matroids and O(D√K·polylog(T)) for transversal matroids via a dynamic approximate maximum-weight basis maintenance technique based on feature rounding and minimum hitting sets, while preserving CUCB's asymptotically tight gap-dependent regret bound.
limitations: The per-round time complexity grows as polylog(T), so for sufficiently long horizons the algorithm becomes slower than CUCB (the authors suggest a hybrid fallback to CUCB). The technique is specific to UCB-style 2D feature decompositions (empirical mean + confidence radius) and has not been extended to other weight structures such as gradient-based or follow-the-perturbed-leader, nor to nonstationary or best-arm-identification settings.
surprise_factor: The main conceptual surprise is that replacing the exact maximum-weight basis with a (1+ε)-approximate one maintained dynamically does not degrade the asymptotic regret bound — prior CUCB analysis fundamentally relies on the exact greedy solution, so one would expect approximation to introduce a gap. The combination of feature rounding (reducing distinct features to O(W²) bins) and minimum hitting set (reducing queries to O(W⁴) representative vectors) is a clean and somewhat unexpected way to make the dynamic data-structure approach compatible with the all-arms-change-simultaneously nature of UCB updates.

key_contribution: SelfPAD, a two-stage framework that leverages weakly-supervised contrastive learning on the Patented Antibody Database (PAD) to learn functionally-informed antibody representations, followed by supervised fine-tuning for humanness prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance on five of six external immunogenicity evaluation tasks.
limitations: The PAD is a noisy dataset with unreliable functional annotations (potential targets) and is biased toward lab-optimized rather than natural sequences, limiting generalizability. The evaluation relies on relatively small external datasets (especially the 25-pair humanization set), and the framework has not yet been extended to other developability properties beyond humanness.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is conceptual rather than numerical: a noisier, smaller patent dataset with weak functional labels consistently outperforms methods trained on the much larger OAS database across five of six evaluation tasks, suggesting that functional grounding via contrastive grouping is more informative than sequence-completion pre-training on scale. However, the margins are moderate (e.g., ~6 F1 points over AbNatiV on the PAD test set) and the perfect scores on the 25-pair humanization dataset rest on a very small sample, so the overall surprise is tempered.

key_contribution: SEIKO, a feedback-efficient online fine-tuning algorithm for diffusion models that interleaves iterative reward learning with KL-regularized optimistic exploration, providing a provable regret guarantee (Õ(d/√K) for linear reward models) while a bridge-preserving property constrains generation to the feasible manifold.
limitations: The paper lacks an explicit limitations section; the Future Work paragraph indicates plans to extend to more specialized biological/chemical diffusion models, suggesting current experiments are limited to relatively small-scale tasks (GFP sequences of length 237, aesthetic scores on Stable Diffusion v1.5, QED for molecules). The method requires solving a trajectory-level control problem at each iteration, which is computationally expensive, and the cleanest regret characterization (Corollary 1) is for linear reward models.
surprise_factor: No particularly surprising findings — the consistent outperformance over non-adaptive, guidance, and PPO baselines across three domains is expected given the theoretical framework, and the margins (e.g., 8.17 vs 7.22 for images, 3.84 vs 3.66 for proteins) are solid but not dramatic. The bridge-preserving property is elegant but follows naturally from the KL structure.

key_contribution: Introduces the human generalization function as a formal framework for modeling how humans form beliefs about LLM capabilities from limited interactions, collects 19K empirical examples showing the function is predictable (BERT achieves best AUC 0.812), and demonstrates that more capable models like GPT-4 can be less aligned with human generalizations in high-stakes deployment settings where the cost of mistakes is high.
limitations: The human generalization function is modeled in the aggregate rather than capturing individual heterogeneity, data collection is restricted to single-question generalizations (not multi-question belief updates), and the function is assumed static over time despite likely evolving as users gain experience with LLMs.
surprise_factor: Two findings stand out: (1) BERT-base outperforms GPT-4 and Llama-2-13B at predicting human belief changes (AUC 0.81 vs. 0.64/0.79), a conceptual surprise that challenges the assumption that larger models capture all relevant linguistic structure; (2) in the highest-stakes deployment setting, GPT-4 has the worst weighted generalized accuracy while smaller 7B models perform comparably or better—a result surprise that inverts the typical 'bigger is better' narrative. The BERT result is somewhat caveated by the authors (different prompting might help LLMs), and the alignment result depends on BERT as a proxy for human beliefs, tempering the surprise somewhat.

key_contribution: Establishes order-optimal sample complexity Õ((H³/ε)^(2+2d/α)) for reward-free RL with kernel-based function approximation under polynomial eigendecay kernels (including Matérn and Neural Tangent kernels), via an adaptive domain partitioning technique and an uncertainty-driven hypothetical exploration reward, closing a gap where prior kernel-based results were unbounded for this kernel class.
limitations: The dependence on episode length H (H³ factor) is explicitly noted as unresolved and potentially improvable. The analysis assumes a hypercubical state-action domain and deterministic rewards, and requires transition probabilities to lie in the RKHS unit ball, which, while mild, restricts applicability to certain MDP structures.
surprise_factor: No particularly surprising findings — the main contribution is a clean theoretical extension showing that the domain partitioning technique from kernelized bandits transfers to the episodic RL setting to recover order-optimal rates for polynomial eigendecay kernels, which is a natural but non-trivial technical achievement given the temporal dependence in RL.

title: Acquisition Conditioned Oracle for Nongreedy Active Feature Acquisition
task_novelty_note: Extends AFA from prediction to decision-making (maximizing expected outcomes), framed as 'less-explored' and 'previously understudied.'

builds_on.title: Imitation learning by coaching
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We offer an alternative perspective by defining an oracle which solves a novel AFA objective meant to balance the limitations posed by the (full) RL and greedy approaches. We argue that our oracle improves on the oracle defined by eq. (1) by being: 1. Non-greedy... 2. Deployable' — the ACO is explicitly a generalization of the forward-selection oracle from this work.

builds_on.title: Optimal dynamic treatment regimes
builds_on.evidence: The decision-making extension (Section 3.6) builds on the DTR/ITR framework: 'The construction of policies to make optimal decisions from data with fully observed contexts has been extensively studied... under the titles dynamic treatment regimes (DTRs) or individualized treatment rules ITRs) (Murphy, 2003; Kosorok & Laber, 2019)' and the policy π_A(x_o) is derived from this framework.

compares_to.title: Joint active feature acquisition and classification with variable-size set encoding
compares_to.evidence: JAFA is listed as a comparison baseline in Fig. 2 (Real-World datasets), Fig. 3 (Cube), and Fig. 4 (Cube) with accuracy vs. cost curves.

compares_to.title: Active feature acquisition with generative surrogate models
compares_to.evidence: GSMRL and GSM+Greedy from this paper are compared in Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 4, and Fig. 5 (Big 5) with accuracy vs. cost curves.

compares_to.title: Eddi: Efficient dynamic discovery of high-value information with partial vae
compares_to.evidence: EDDI is listed as a comparison baseline in Fig. 2 (Real-World datasets) with accuracy vs. cost curves.

compares_to.title: Learning to maximize mutual information for dynamic feature selection
compares_to.evidence: AMOPT is compared in Fig. 6 (786d MNIST) where the paper states 'we find comparable SOTA from the AACO policy' against AMOPT's greedy policy.

key_contribution: Introduces the Acquisition Conditioned Oracle (ACO), a nonparametric, non-greedy, and deployable oracle-based policy for active feature acquisition that minimizes expected prediction loss over subsets of remaining features (penalized by cost) using only observed information, achieving SOTA performance across prediction and decision-making benchmarks with simple kNN density estimates and random subset sampling.
limitations: The authors note that further work is needed to characterize when the ACO is strictly suboptimal relative to the full AFA MDP, and that the approximations (kNN for conditional distributions, random subset sampling) are elementary, leaving open whether more sophisticated approximations could yield additional gains. Additionally, the decision-making extension is demonstrated on only one synthetic environment and one real-world dataset, and the method's higher inference-time complexity (O(nd|O|m)) compared to parametric RL policies (O(m)) may limit applicability in latency-critical settings.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that a deliberately simple nonparametric oracle—kNN for conditional distributions, ~100 random subsets for the combinatorial search, and gradient boosted trees for prediction—matches or beats deep RL and generative-model AFA methods across multiple benchmarks, including scaling to 784-d MNIST on par with the amortized-optimization SOTA (AMOPT). This challenges the implicit assumption in the AFA literature that complex learned policies or surrogate generative models are necessary to navigate the acquisition space effectively.

title: Position: Why Tabular Foundation Models Should Be a Research Priority
task_novelty_note: Authors explicitly coin 'LTM' and frame tabular foundation models as 'almost entirely unexplored,' introducing a new problem formulation with four desiderata not present in prior cross-table or tabular-generation work.
key_contribution: Coins the term 'Large Tabular Model' (LTM) and provides a formal four-desiderata framework (mixed-type columns, cross-dataset modelling, textual context, column-order invariance) arguing that tabular foundation models are an underexplored, high-impact, and computationally accessible research priority for the ML community.
limitations: As a position paper, it proposes no new method, benchmark, or empirical result, so its impact depends entirely on whether the community adopts the LTM framing. The authors themselves note that the diversity, quality, and bias of existing tabular corpora (e.g., TabLib) remain unverified, that reliable intrinsic evaluation metrics for LTMs do not yet exist, and that the extent to which LTMs will generalize to sensitive domains such as healthcare is unknown.
surprise_factor: No empirical findings to assess for surprise, as this is a position paper. The most striking conceptual claim is that LLMs are fundamentally inefficient for tabular generation (a single Gaussian variable requires a complex autoregressive token sequence), but this is a well-motivated architectural argument rather than a surprising experimental result.

title: Piecewise Constant and Linear Regression Trees: An Optimal Dynamic Programming Approach
authors: Jacobus G. M. van der Linden

task_novelty_note: Optimal regression trees are a well-established task (NP-hard since 1976; MIP formulations since 2017); the contribution is new DP methods, not a new problem.

key_contribution: Three new dynamic programming algorithms for optimal regression trees (piecewise constant, simple linear, and multiple linear) that exploit a depth-two precomputation trick to achieve 1–2 orders of magnitude scalability improvement over prior optimal methods, while providing the first optimal DP formulations for piecewise linear regression trees.
limitations: The methods scale exponentially with the number of features, and no depth-two shortcut exists for multiple linear regression (SRT-L) because the per-instance cost decomposition is intractable. The paper acknowledges that binarization strategy and complexity-tuning (joint optimization of tree size and leaf model complexity) remain underexplored, and that extending to non-binary split predicates and parallelizing the DP remain open.
surprise_factor: The 1–2 order-of-magnitude scalability gain is substantial but well-explained by the depth-two precomputation, so it is not deeply surprising. A mildly interesting finding is that SRT-SL (simple linear regression in leaves) runs at nearly the same speed as SRT-C (constant predictors), suggesting the per-instance cost decomposition for linear regression is as efficient as the constant case in practice.

title: Algorithm and Hardness for Dynamic Attention Maintenance in Large Language Models
input: single-entry update (i, j, δ) to K or V
task_novelty_note: Extends static attention computation (Zandieh 2023, Alman & Song 2023) to a dynamic/online setting with single-entry updates.
key_contribution: Formally defines the dynamic (online) attention matrix-vector multiplication problem (ODAMV) and provides a lazy-update data structure with O(n^{ω(1,1,a)−a}) amortized update time and O(n^a) worst-case query time, along with a matching conditional lower bound under the Hinted Matrix-Vector (HMV) conjecture, establishing the first tight complexity characterization for dynamic attention maintenance.
limitations: The lower bound is conditional on the HMV conjecture; an unconditional lower bound remains an open problem. The problem formulation is restricted to single-entry updates to K or V per iteration, whereas practical LLM training may involve simultaneous multi-entry updates to both matrices.
surprise_factor: No particularly surprising findings — the matching upper and conditional lower bounds are the expected outcome of applying a well-established lazy-update framework to a newly formalized problem. The conceptual contribution is the clean identification of HMV-conjecture hardness (as opposed to fine-grained complexity hardness) as the right lens for dynamic attention, which is a natural but previously unexplored connection.

title: Proactive DP: A Multiple Target Optimization Framework for DP-SGD
output: optimized DP-SGD parameters (σ, T, s, step size)
task_novelty_note: DP-SGD training is well-established since Abadi et al. 2016; the paper contributes a new parameter-selection framework (proactive DP) for this existing task.

builds_on.title: Deep learning with differential privacy
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We non-trivially improve the analysis of the moment accountant method in (Abadi et al., 2016)' and directly extends their Theorem B.1 with explicit constants

builds_on.title: Gaussian differential privacy
builds_on.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society 2021
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'we leverage the findings from f-DP (Dong et al., 2021)' and uses the f-DP framework to prove tightness of the moment accountant bound (Theorem 3.2)

builds_on.title: Hogwild: A lockfree approach to parallelizing stochastic gradient descent
builds_on.evidence: Appendix A states the asynchronous framework 'is based on the Hogwild! (Recht et al., 2011) recursion' and the algorithm follows Hogwild's philosophy for asynchronous SGD

compares_to.title: Deep learning with differential privacy
compares_to.evidence: Section 5 compares test accuracy at ε=2, k=7 epochs: 'we achieved ≈60% test accuracy... In Figure 6.1 of Abadi's paper, they also achieved around 60% test accuracy after 7 epochs' with 14.14% vs 26% accuracy deduction

compares_to.title: Unlocking high-accuracy differentially private image classification through scale
compares_to.evidence: Section 5 states 'Even with the state-of-the-art method of (De et al., 2022) only achieves 65.9% for CIFAR10 without pretraining data' and compares accuracy deductions (32.1% vs 14.14%)

key_contribution: Introduces proactive DP, a framework that inverts traditional DP accounting to enable a priori selection of all DP-SGD parameters via a tight closed-form guarantee σ = √(2(ε+ln(1/δ))/ε) with T ≥ γθ²k²/ε (proven tight up to a constant factor ≈4 via f-DP), combined with a utility graph and DP calculator to jointly optimize privacy, utility, and implementation goals before training.
limitations: The utility graph is explicitly a heuristic best-case estimate that does not guarantee the true DP-SGD accuracy will match predictions, and experimental validation is limited to simple problems (logistic regression on LIBSVM, LeNet on MNIST) with small privacy budgets (ε ≤ 0.15), leaving open whether the framework scales to large architectures and complex datasets. The main readable theorem (Theorem 3.1) is restricted to ε < 0.5, and the asynchronous setting assumes iid local data sets across clients.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that the moment accountant method, previously known only to give loose bounds with unspecified constants, admits a remarkably simple closed-form guarantee σ = √(2(ε + ln(1/δ))/ε) that is provably tight up to a constant factor of ~4 in T. This is a genuine analytical breakthrough, but the experimental evidence is limited to small-scale problems (LeNet/MNIST, logistic regression/LIBSVM), so the practical impact at scale remains unvalidated.

title: On the Independence Assumption in Neurosymbolic Learning
task_novelty_note: Neurosymbolic learning with logical constraints is a well-established task; the paper analyzes a foundational assumption within it rather than introducing a new problem formulation.
key_contribution: Proves that the conditional independence assumption in probabilistic neurosymbolic learning systematically biases models toward deterministic solutions (preventing uncertainty quantification) and produces non-convex, disconnected loss landscapes, using a geometric characterisation via boolean implicants and cubical sets from computational homology.
limitations: The empirical validation is limited to a toy traffic-light example and MNIST Addition, so the practical magnitude of the identified effects in larger, more complex settings remains untested. The paper does not propose a concrete practical method to replace the independence assumption; it notes that dropping independence makes inference much more complex and that mixtures of independents may require exponentially many components for tasks like MNIST Addition.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is significant: the independence assumption, adopted almost universally in PNL for computational tractability, is proven to be the very source of both overconfidence (bias toward deterministic solutions) and optimization difficulty (non-convex, disconnected minima). The clean dichotomy—semantic loss is convex over expressive distributions but generically non-convex over independent ones—challenges the field's working assumption that independence is a benign simplification. However, the empirical validation is limited to a toy traffic-light example and MNIST Addition, so the practical magnitude of these effects in larger settings remains untested.

title: When Representations Align: Universality in Representation Learning Dynamics
task_novelty_note: Understanding representation learning dynamics is a well-established task; the paper provides a new architecture-agnostic effective theory for it.

builds_on.title: The local elasticity of neural networks
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'One motivating factor for the method used here is the empirical phenomenon of local elasticity... This allows us to consider neural network learning dynamics as a local process, suggesting that the local interaction between representations may already provide insight into the behavior of the entire dataset.' The entire two-point interaction model relies on this property to justify reducing full-dataset dynamics to pairwise interactions.

key_contribution: Derives an architecture-agnostic effective theory of representation learning by modeling pairwise datapoint interactions through smoothness constraints on encoder and decoder maps, reducing dynamics to a 3-dimensional ODE system with only two fitted effective learning rates, and showing it captures universal behaviors including the rich/lazy learning distinction across diverse deep network architectures.
limitations: The two-point interaction framework has no clear path to extension to larger datasets, and the theory does not account for architecture-specific inductive biases (e.g., convolutional structure, attention) that interact with the modeled dynamics. The theory also fails for low-expressivity architectures (e.g., 2-layer networks), and MNIST representational structure predictions require an ad-hoc exponential weighing procedure to handle geometric inconsistencies like the triangle inequality.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that smoothness constraints plus gradient descent alone—without any architecture-specific inductive bias—reproduce the rich/lazy distinction and structured representational learning (feature collapse, XOR merging) across diverse architectures, with only two free parameters. However, the empirical validation is confined to two-point datasets, XOR, and small blob datasets, with MNIST results being qualitative and requiring ad-hoc exponential weighing to handle geometric inconsistencies, which tempers the universality claim.

title: Forget Sharpness: Perturbed Forgetting of Model Biases Within SAM Dynamics
task_novelty_note: Image classification and robustness evaluation are well-established tasks; the contribution is a new training perturbation and mechanistic perspective, not a new problem formulation.

builds_on.title: Sharpness-aware minimization for efficiently improving generalization
builds_on.evidence: The OBF perturbation is a direct modification of SAM's perturbation step; the paper states 'we propose an output bias forgetting (OBF) perturbation' within SAM dynamics, and the algorithm (Algorithm A.1) operates within SAM's two-step update structure.

compares_to.title: Sharpness-aware minimization for efficiently improving generalization
compares_to.evidence: Standard SAM with steepest ascent (STEEP) perturbation is listed in Tables 1 and B.1 as a baseline with accuracy and sharpness numbers alongside the proposed OBF perturbation.

compares_to.title: Surrogate gap minimization improves sharpness-aware training
compares_to.evidence: GSAM with steepest ascent perturbation is listed in Tables 1 and B.1 as a baseline with accuracy and sharpness numbers alongside the proposed OBF perturbation.

compares_to.title: ASAM: Adaptive sharpness-aware minimization for scale-invariant learning of deep neural networks
compares_to.evidence: ASAM with steepest ascent perturbation is listed in Table B.1 as a baseline with accuracy and sharpness numbers alongside the proposed OBF perturbation.

compares_to.title: On warm-starting neural network training
compares_to.evidence: Shrink-and-perturb (Ash & Adams, 2020) is listed in Table B.1 as a baseline with accuracy and sharpness numbers for empirical comparison against the proposed OBF perturbation.

key_contribution: Reframes SAM's perturbation step as 'perturbed forgetting' of model biases via the information bottleneck principle, and proposes an Output Bias Forgetting (OBF) perturbation that targets biases exposed through model outputs rather than steepest gradient directions, outperforming standard SAM, GSAM, and ASAM on ImageNet and robustness benchmarks while sometimes converging to sharper regions.
limitations: The paper is limited to image classification experiments with ViTs and ResNets, and the authors explicitly state they do not claim OBF is optimal for all settings. The theoretical connection to the information bottleneck principle relies on conjectures rather than formal proofs, and characterizing the exact nature of biases targeted by different perturbations is left as future work.
surprise_factor: The conceptual surprise is that OBF outperforms steepest-ascent SAM by 1.5–2.5% on ImageNet while sometimes converging to substantially sharper minima (e.g., ViT-S/16: sharpness 17.1 vs. 2.4 for steepest ascent, yet higher accuracy), directly contradicting the flatness narrative. This is well-supported across four architectures, five evaluation sets, and a correlation analysis, making it a credible challenge to a widely-held assumption rather than a single anomalous result.

title: Generalized Smooth Variational Inequalities: Methods with Adaptive Stepsizes
task_novelty_note: Extends VI solving from Lipschitz + strongly monotone operators to the broader α-symmetric + p-quasi sharp class.

builds_on.title: The extragradient method for finding saddle points and other problems
builds_on.evidence: Paper directly extends the Korpelevich (extragradient) method with adaptive stepsizes for α-symmetric and p-quasi sharp operators, proving new convergence guarantees (Theorems 5.2, 5.3, 7.1, 7.3)

builds_on.title: A modification of the arrow-hurwicz method for search of saddle points
builds_on.venue: Mathematical notes of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR 1980
builds_on.evidence: Paper directly extends the Popov (optimistic gradient) method with adaptive stepsizes for α-symmetric and p-quasi sharp operators, proving new convergence guarantees (Theorems 6.2, 6.3)

builds_on.title: Generalized-smooth nonconvex optimization is as efficient as smooth nonconvex optimization
builds_on.evidence: Paper adopts the α-symmetric operator class from this work as its core smoothness assumption (Assumption 2.1) and uses Proposition 2.2 from this paper for the analysis

builds_on.title: Last iterate convergence of Popov method for non-monotone stochastic variational inequalities
builds_on.evidence: Paper adopts the p-quasi sharpness property (Assumption 2.4) from this work as its core monotonicity assumption and uses the example operator from Proposition 2.5

compares_to.title: Solving nonconvex-nonconcave min-max problems exhibiting weak minty solutions
compares_to.evidence: Korpelevich method with golden ratio stepsizes from this paper appears as a baseline in Figures 1 and 2, where the paper's adaptive stepsizes are shown to outperform it for all three (α,p) settings

key_contribution: First convergence guarantees for projection, Korpelevich (extragradient), and Popov (optimistic gradient) methods on variational inequalities with α-symmetric generalized smoothness and p-quasi sharp operators, using adaptive stepsizes that yield a rate of O(k^{-2/(p-2)}) for p>2, improving upon the prior O(k^{-1/(p-1)}) under stronger monotonicity and Lipschitz assumptions.
limitations: The authors identify two directions for future work: extending the analysis to weak Minty conditions and to stochastic VIs. Additionally, all numerical experiments are conducted on 2D toy operators and a 2D ring GAN dataset, leaving open the question of scalability to high-dimensional or large-scale ML problems; the theoretical adaptive stepsizes also require knowledge of problem parameters (p, α, L₀, L₁) in their non-backtracking form.
surprise_factor: The rate improvement from O(k^{-1/(p-1)}) to O(k^{-2/(p-2)}) for p>2 under weaker assumptions is a clean theoretical gain but not dramatically surprising given the structure of the descent inequalities. The more notable practical observation is that the simple projection method with parameter-free adaptive stepsizes outperforms the more sophisticated Korpelevich and Popov methods in experiments when α and p are large, since the latter's stepsizes shrink with problem constants while the former's do not — a somewhat counterintuitive result for a method known to diverge on monotone VIs.

title: Discovering Mixtures of Structural Causal Models from Time Series Data
task_novelty_note: Extends mixture causal discovery (prior: independent data) and time series causal discovery (prior: single model) to their intersection: mixtures of SCMs from time series.

compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1 (Netsim-mixture and DREAM3) and Table 2 (Netsim) as PCMCI+ with variants -s, -o, -g, with AUROC and F1 scores alongside MCD.

compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 1, Table 2, and synthetic dataset figures (Figure 4, 9, 10) as Rhino with AUROC and F1 scores alongside MCD.

key_contribution: A variational inference framework (MCD) that jointly discovers K structural causal models and per-sample mixture membership from heterogeneous multivariate time series, with provable identifiability conditions for both linear Gaussian SVARs and general SCMs, outperforming state-of-the-art single-model baselines on synthetic and real-world datasets.
limitations: The method assumes causal sufficiency (no latent confounders) and requires the number of mixture components K as a hyperparameter. When underlying causal graphs are highly similar (as in the Netsim non-mixture setup), the mixture model can underperform single-graph baselines due to sample complexity, and the authors note that future work is needed to handle latent confounders and non-stationarity within components.
surprise_factor: The most genuinely surprising finding is that MCD-Nonlinear performs *better* when the number of mixture components K is over-specified (K > K*), with additional SCMs acting as 'buffers' that help the optimization converge to the correct grouping — counterintuitive given that extra parameters typically hurt. The 95.6% clustering accuracy on DREAM3 despite all methods scoring near-random on causal discovery F1 is also notable, suggesting the mixture structure is easier to recover than the individual graphs.

title: Statistically Optimal Generative Modeling with Maximum Deviation from the Empirical Distribution
task_novelty_note: Generative modeling is a well-established task; the paper provides new theoretical guarantees (non-replication bounds) and a penalty for an already-accepted problem.

builds_on.title: Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We introduce LIPERM (Left-Inverse Penalized Empirical Risk Minimizer), a penalized version of WGAN that favors left invertibility of the pushforward map'

builds_on.title: Improved Training of Wasserstein GANs
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Our implementation follows the pseudo-code presented in Algorithm 1, and is inspired by the code accompanying (Gulrajani et al., 2017)... We add the LIPERM penalization to the objective function of the WGANs'

key_contribution: First finite-sample lower bound proving that a generative model whose push-forward map has a smooth left inverse (enforced via the LIPERM penalty on WGAN) is separated from the empirical distribution by at least order n^{-1/d}—the minimax-optimal rate—while simultaneously achieving minimax-optimal precision toward the true distribution, thereby providing a mathematical guarantee of non-replication without sacrificing statistical efficiency.
limitations: The paper does not address the choice of latent dimension d, and extending the analysis to diffusion models, higher-smoothness function classes, or non-IPM distances (e.g., Sinkhorn divergence) is left as future work. Empirically, on standard datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10, Swiss Roll) the authors could not demonstrate visible creativity gains because replication was not an observed issue with the tested architectures, and Swiss Roll training instability persisted regardless of the penalty.
surprise_factor: The main conceptual insight is that left-invertibility places the generator at the *maximum* possible distance from the empirical distribution (n^{-1/d}) while retaining minimax-optimal precision — meaning the anti-overfitting constraint is exactly the one compatible with optimal learning, not a trade-off. This is a clean theoretical result, though the empirical evidence is modest: the authors acknowledge they could not observe creativity improvements on standard benchmarks, and the Swiss Roll experiments showed the penalty does not fix training instability.

title: Optimization without Retraction on the Random Generalized Stiefel Manifold
input: random estimates B_ζ of constraint matrix
output: matrix X on generalized Stiefel manifold
task_novelty_note: Extends optimization on the generalized Stiefel manifold from deterministic B to stochastic B (random feasible set), a setting the authors note lacks existing techniques.

builds_on.title: Fast and accurate optimization on the orthogonal manifold without retraction
builds_on.evidence: Paper states the method 'is inspired by a recent line of work that first considered the orthogonal group St_{I_n}(n,n) (Ablin & Peyré, 2022)' and extends the landing iteration from the orthogonal group to the generalized Stiefel manifold.

builds_on.title: Optimization flows landing on the Stiefel manifold
builds_on.evidence: Paper states the landing method 'was later extended to the Stiefel manifold St_{I_n}(p,n) (Gao et al., 2022b)' and this work further extends it to the generalized Stiefel manifold with stochastic constraints.

builds_on.title: Orthogonal Directions Constrained Gradient Method: From non-linear equality constraints to Stiefel manifold
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'The theory presented here improves on that of Schechtman et al. (2023) in two important directions' — introducing relative ascent directions and removing the requirement that noise be in the tangent space via a smooth merit function.

compares_to.title: Cholesky QR-based retraction on the generalized Stiefel manifold
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Figure 2 as 'Riemannian steepest descent with QR-based Cholesky retraction (Sato & Aihara, 2019)' with timing and convergence results alongside the proposed landing method.

compares_to.title: An orthogonalization-free parallelizable framework for all-electron calculations in density functional theory
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Figure 2 as 'the PLAM method (Gao et al., 2022a)' with timing and convergence results alongside the proposed landing method for the GEVP experiment.

key_contribution: Extends the retraction-free landing method to the generalized Stiefel manifold with a stochastic constraint matrix B, using Fletcher's augmented Lagrangian as a smooth merit function to prove O(1/K) (deterministic) and O(1/√K) (stochastic) convergence to critical points while requiring only matrix multiplications and never forming B explicitly.
limitations: In the stochastic case, convergence requires the assumption that line segments between successive iterates remain within the ε-safe region with probability one, which cannot be guaranteed without additional distributional assumptions on the noise. The method is restricted to smooth equality constraints defining a manifold and does not extend to inequality constraints or non-smooth objectives.
surprise_factor: The main conceptual surprise is that a method requiring only matrix multiplications—no factorizations, no explicit formation of B—achieves the same convergence rates as full Riemannian optimization while naturally handling stochastic constraints. The theoretical insight that Fletcher's augmented Lagrangian serves as a valid smooth merit function for the landing field (enabling the stochastic analysis that Schechtman et al.'s non-smooth merit function could not support) is a clean and non-obvious contribution, though the practical speedups are largely expected given the avoidance of expensive linear algebra.

title: A Probabilistic Approach to Learning the Degree of Equivariance in Steerable CNNs
task_novelty_note: Learning the degree of equivariance in equivariant networks is well-established (Partial GCNNs, RPPs, RSteer); this paper offers a new SCNN-native method with interpretability.

builds_on.title: A program to build E(n)-equivariant steerable CNNs
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Building upon the SCNN framework developed by Cesa et al. (2022)' and 'Our implementation relies on the escnn library (Cesa et al., 2022), providing an intuitive environment for configuring SCNNs'

builds_on.title: Steerable CNNs
builds_on.evidence: The entire method is formulated within the SCNN framework; paper states 'Despite the flexibility of the framework of steerable CNNs (Cohen & Welling, 2016b) compared to GCNNs, only very few methods are compatible with this framework'

compares_to.title: Residual pathway priors for soft equivariance constraints
compares_to.evidence: Listed as 'RPP' baseline in Tables 1, 2, 3, and 5 with accuracy/RMSE numbers alongside the proposed method

compares_to.title: Approximately equivariant networks for imperfectly symmetric dynamics
compares_to.evidence: Listed as 'RSteer' baseline in Table 3 with RMSE numbers; paper states 'we simply port their best RSteer configuration as reported by their repository, to our approach'

compares_to.title: General E(2)-equivariant steerable CNNs
compares_to.evidence: Listed as 'Restriction' baseline in Tables 1 and 5; paper states 'regular SCNNs with pre-tuned degrees of equivariance through group restrictions (Weiler & Cesa, 2019)'

key_contribution: A probabilistic method that learns the degree of equivariance in Steerable CNNs by replacing the uniform group-averaging in kernel projection with a learnable likelihood distribution parameterised via Fourier coefficients, yielding an interpretable, layer-wise equivariance degree with competitive performance on partially symmetric datasets.
limitations: The approach is restricted to compact groups and cannot model partial translation equivariance; it uses significantly more parameters than regular SCNNs even with band-limiting, requires recomputing the steerable basis after each forward pass, and needs additional hyperparameters for alignment and KL-divergence regularisation. No theoretical guarantee is provided that the learnt likelihood corresponds to the true data symmetry.
surprise_factor: No particularly surprising findings — the performance improvements over baselines are modest and consistent with expectations. The most notable practical insight is that PSCNNs, which initialise as fully equivariant, struggle on non-symmetric data with small training sets (unlike CNNs or RPPs that start non-equivariant), highlighting a trade-off between the inductive bias benefit and the cost of breaking equivariance from scratch.

surprise_factor: The finding that the stochasticity correction to test risk vanishes entirely in the overparametrized regime (α > 1) at infinite time, while persisting in the underparametrized regime, is a clean conceptual result: stochasticity does not degrade generalization once the model can interpolate. The practical detail that a simple verification pipeline with 2 expert and 100 random trajectories is sufficient to catch most false-positive scripts is a useful but not surprising engineering observation.

title: Position: An Inner Interpretability Framework for AI Inspired by Lessons from Cognitive Neuroscience
task_novelty_note: Mechanistic interpretability of AI systems is a well-established task; the paper contributes a conceptual framework for how to conduct it, not a new task formulation.
key_contribution: Proposes a four-level multilevel conceptual framework (computational, algorithmic, primitive, implementation) adapted from Marr & Poggio's Cognitive Neuroscience framework, with concrete methodological strategies (severe testing, mutual constraints across levels, invariance testing) for building and evaluating mechanistic explanations in AI Inner Interpretability, illustrated end-to-end with factual recall in language transformers.
limitations: As a position paper, the framework is not empirically validated; its applicability is demonstrated only through a single running example (factual recall) and its effectiveness in improving interpretability outcomes remains speculative. The authors explicitly note that adapting the learning and evolution levels of the multilevel framework to artificial systems requires future work, and that other lines of research (training data curation, carbon emissions) are more urgent for addressing AI safety and efficiency concerns.
surprise_factor: The main conceptual insight—that the specific methodological pathologies plaguing AI Inner Interpretability (incomplete mechanisms, arbitrary abstraction levels, unexamined assumptions in bottom-up approaches) are essentially identical to problems Cognitive Neuroscience confronted decades ago and has developed structured solutions for—is a useful reframe but not a genuine surprise to anyone familiar with both fields. No empirical results are presented, so there is no result-level surprise.

key_contribution: A quantitative probabilistic forecast showing that, if current LLM scaling trends continue, models will be trained on datasets as large as the total stock of public human-generated text (median ~510T tokens for the indexed web) between 2026 and 2032 (median 2028), and a systematic survey of potential circumvention strategies including synthetic data, multimodal transfer learning, non-public data, and data efficiency improvements.
limitations: The paper's arguments about alternative data sources (synthetic data, transfer learning, non-public data) are explicitly described as 'mostly qualitative' and lack quantitative scaling estimates. The model relies on several strong assumptions—constant per-user data production, Common Crawl as a representative sample of the indexed web, and linear extrapolation of dataset growth—that introduce substantial uncertainty, as reflected in the wide 95% confidence intervals (e.g., indexed web stock: 130T–2100T tokens).
surprise_factor: The median exhaustion year of 2028 is earlier than the qualitative 'sometime this decade' framing many in the field had assumed, and the indexed web stock (~510T tokens median) is smaller than intuition might suggest given the perceived vastness of the web. However, the wide 95% CI (2026–2032) and the many compounding assumptions (constant per-user data production, representative Common Crawl sampling, linear extrapolation of dataset growth) temper the surprise considerably.

key_contribution: A comprehensive empirical comparison of ConvNeXt and ViT architectures under supervised and CLIP training paradigms, matched in size and ImageNet accuracy, revealing substantial differences in error types, calibration, robustness, transferability, shape/texture bias, synthetic data performance, and transformation invariance that are invisible to the standard ImageNet accuracy metric.
limitations: The analysis is limited to base-sized models pretrained on LAION-400M for CLIP, and the authors cannot control for the number and quality of pretraining data since they use publicly available pretrained checkpoints. Self-supervised models are excluded from the main comparison, and the robustness benchmarks share ImageNet's class taxonomy, potentially overstating supervised models' advantage.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is that supervised ConvNeXt achieves VTAB transferability (71.0) nearly identical to CLIP models (72.2), challenging the assumption that CLIP's diverse image-text pretraining is essential for strong transfer—a result that holds across all three VTAB subgroups. Additionally, the calibration result that ConvNeXt outperforms ViT (contradicting Minderer et al. 2021) and that CLIP models are systematically overconfident while supervised models are slightly underconfident on OOD data are conceptual surprises that shift attribution from architecture to training objective.

title: CF-OPT: Counterfactual Explanations for Structured Prediction
input: alternative decision y^alt or regret threshold ε
task_novelty_note: Extends counterfactual explanations for structured prediction (Forel et al. 2023, restricted to RF/kNN) to general deep models with black-box optimization layers, and introduces the novel ε-explanation type.

builds_on.title: Auto-encoding variational bayes
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'We build upon variational autoencoders a principled way of obtaining counterfactuals' and modifies the VAE training objective with a cost-aware loss (Eq. 6)

builds_on.title: Explainable data-driven optimization: From context to decision and back again
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'our setting extends the one of Forel et al. (2023), who provide explanations for a restricted type of pipeline based on random forests and k-nearest neighbors'

builds_on.title: Constrained differential optimization
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'Our algorithm to obtain explanations is based on constrained differential optimization and, in particular, the modified differential method of multipliers (MDMM) of Platt & Barr (1987)'

key_contribution: CF-OPT, a first-order optimization algorithm that finds plausible counterfactual explanations for structured learning pipelines (deep prediction model + black-box optimization layer) by searching in the latent space of a cost-aware VAE with a latent hypersphere plausibility regularization, avoiding the adversarial artifacts produced by naive feature-space search in high-dimensional settings.
limitations: The method requires continuous input features, limiting its applicability to categorical or discrete covariates. The approach relies on a VAE as the generative model for plausibility modeling, and the authors identify exploring alternative generative models such as diffusion models as a promising future direction.
surprise_factor: No particularly surprising findings. The connection between naive counterfactuals and adversarial examples in high dimensions is well-documented in the classification literature and is confirmed here for structured prediction. The cost-aware VAE loss showing that increasing α also improves feature reconstruction (not just cost reconstruction) is a mildly interesting side effect, but the overall contribution is a well-executed combination of known components (VAE, MDMM, regularization) applied to a new setting.

title: Parameter Estimation in DAGs from Incomplete Data via Optimal Transport
task_novelty_note: Parameter estimation in DAGs from incomplete data is a decades-old task (EM 1977, VI 1999); the paper contributes a new OT-based method rather than a new problem formulation.

builds_on.title: Wasserstein auto-encoders
builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'OTP-DAG in fact serves as an extension of WAE for learning general directed graphical models' and 'our theoretical development renders a tractable formulation of the Wasserstein objective for models with latent variables, which is established as a generalization for the WAE model.'

compares_to.title: Maximum Likelihood from Incomplete Data Via the EM Algorithm
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Tables 1, 2, and 3 as 'Batch EM' and 'EM' baselines with numerical results alongside OTP-DAG.

compares_to.title: Stochastic variational inference
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Tables 1 and 2 as 'SVI' baseline with numerical results alongside OTP-DAG.

compares_to.title: Autoencoding variational inference for topic models
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Tables 1 and 2 as 'ProdLDA' baseline with numerical results alongside OTP-DAG.

compares_to.title: Neural discrete representation learning
compares_to.evidence: Listed in Table 4 as 'VQ-VAE' baseline with SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS, rFID, and Perplexity results alongside OTP-DAG.

key_contribution: Introduces OTP-DAG, an optimal transport framework that reformulates parameter estimation in arbitrary directed acyclic graphical models with latent variables as Wasserstein distance minimization, proving (Theorem 4.1) that the global OT cost decomposes into local backward maps from observed nodes to their parents, yielding a tractable, assumption-light objective that generalizes Wasserstein Auto-Encoders to general DAGs and empirically recovers ground-truth parameters while outperforming EM, SVI, and VQ-VAE baselines across topic modeling, hidden Markov models, and discrete representation learning.
limitations: Ancestral sampling to evaluate model marginals over parent nodes becomes computationally expensive for larger graphs, and the reparameterization trick required for gradient-based optimization cannot be easily applied to discrete distributions or non-reparameterizable continuous distributions (e.g., Gamma). The exact computation of Wasserstein distance has high complexity in high-dimensional spaces, necessitating approximations such as Sinkhorn divergences or sliced Wasserstein distance.
surprise_factor: The most notable empirical finding is the dramatic reduction in codebook collapse for discrete representation learning (perplexity ~500 vs ~70 for VQ-VAE on CIFAR-10), which the authors attribute to the push-forward divergence being harder to trivially satisfy than a per-sample KL term. However, this is a single comparison against one baseline on four datasets, and the theoretical explanation (Section B) makes the mechanism fairly predictable, so the result is more confirmatory than genuinely surprising. The 5× speedup over EM on HMM is practical but expected given stochastic vs. batch optimization.

title: Optimal Transport for Structure Learning Under Missing Data
task_novelty_note: Causal discovery under missing data is well-studied (Tu et al. 2019, MissDAG 2022, VISL 2022); OTM offers a new OT-based method for this established task.

builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'In the non-linear experiments, we choose DAGMA (Bello et al., 2022) as our base causal discovery framework' and uses its log-det acyclicity regularizer in Eq. (7)

builds_on.evidence: Paper states 'For linear models, we run OTM using NOTEARS (Zheng et al., 2018) as the underlying causal discovery method' and uses its trace-exp acyclicity characterization

builds_on.title: Missing Data Imputation Using Optimal Transport
builds_on.evidence: Paper adapts the OT imputation strategy: 'Muzellec et al. (2020) and Zhao et al. (2023) in particular propose a strategy for learning the imputations by minimizing the OT distance between two pseudo-complete batch of data points' which informs the cost function in Definition 3.1

compares_to.title: MissDAG: Causal Discovery in the Presence of Missing Data with Continuous Additive Noise Models
compares_to.evidence: Paper states 'We further compare OTM with MissDAG (Gao et al., 2022) as the key competing method' and MissDAG appears in all results figures (3-13) with SHD and F1 scores

compares_to.title: Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations
compares_to.evidence: MissForest imputation appears as a baseline in all results figures (3-13) combined with DAGMA for structure learning, with SHD and F1 scores reported alongside OTM

compares_to.title: Missing Data Imputation Using Optimal Transport
compares_to.evidence: OT imputation (Batch Sinkhorn and RoundRobin Sinkhorn) appears as baselines in all results figures (3-13) combined with DAGMA, with SHD and F1 scores reported alongside OTM

key_contribution: Proposes OTM, an optimal transport framework for causal DAG learning under missing data that formulates structure learning as a Wasserstein density-fitting problem with a stochastic correction map jointly optimized with SCM parameters, outperforming EM-based methods (MissDAG) and imputation-then-learn baselines in non-linear settings while offering superior scalability.
limitations: The highly non-convex optimization objective precludes theoretical convergence guarantees, and the framework is currently inapplicable to cyclic causal graphs or graphs with latent confounders. Identifiability under MNAR missingness remains an open problem, as the missingness mechanism cannot be ignored without additional graphical conditions that are practically difficult to obtain.
surprise_factor: The most notable finding is the empirical demonstration (Figure 1 and throughout) that the best imputation method by reconstruction quality (MissForest) does not consistently yield the best causal graph, which challenges the intuitive 'impute well, then discover' pipeline. However, this observation was anticipated by prior work (Kyono et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2022), and the performance gains over MissDAG, while consistent, are moderate rather than dramatic, so the overall surprise is modest.

title: ArtWhisperer: A Dataset for Characterizing Human-AI Interactions in Artistic Creations
task_novelty_note: Authors explicitly frame sequential, goal-directed human-AI interaction with text-to-image models as absent from prior datasets; the steerability metric is a new problem formulation.
